title: What is LinktoDM?
html:
What is LinktoDM?

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Let’s be honest, responding to every Instagram message feels like trying to play whack-a-mole while blindfolded. You reply to one, two more pop up. Story reactions, giveaway questions, random emojis, “Hey, is this still in stock?” messages at 3am. It never stops.

Now imagine you had a friendly assistant who never gets tired, never needs coffee, and somehow knows exactly what to say. That’s LinktoDM. It’s not magic, it’s automation, but it feels like magic when your DMs handle themselves.

At its core, LinktoDM is like the chillest teammate you’ve ever had, the one who handles all the tedious stuff so you can focus on content, strategy, or hey, maybe even sleep. When someone comments “price?” on your latest post, LinktoDM can slide into their DMs with the answer before you’ve even seen the notification.

What you can automate

Section titled “What you can automate”
  • Auto-DM everyone who comments
  • Send a friendly greeting to new followers
  • Ask them to follow you before unlocking a discount code
  • Start convos when someone reacts to a story
  • Capture leads directly inside Instagram

And here’s the kicker: it doesn’t feel robotic. You can write your own messages, add emojis, even randomize replies so it feels fresh every time.

Who it’s for

Section titled “Who it’s for”

LinktoDM works whether you’re managing a personal brand, a boutique candle store, or your dog’s influencer page (no judgment, Biscuit deserves followers).

Real-life examples

Section titled “Real-life examples”
  • Sara, a handmade jewelry seller, uses it to ask every commenter if they want the size guide.
  • Raj, who runs a fitness page, auto-DMs his meal plan to anyone who replies “interested” to his reel.
  • Tina, a skincare brand founder, captures emails via DM using a lead form template

They all save hours a week and don’t miss a single lead.

Setting it up

Section titled “Setting it up”

Honestly, if you’ve ever sent a DM, you can set this up. No code, no flowcharts, no “if-this-then-that” wizardry. It just works. Most users say they’re up and running in under 10 minutes, quicker than making a cup of chai.

Top features

Section titled “Top features”
  • Comment-to-DM Automation
  • Ask to Follow Before Messaging
  • Greeting Messages
  • AI-Powered Replies
  • Click and Conversion Tracking
  • Backtrack Missed Comments

Safe and Meta-compliant

Section titled “Safe and Meta-compliant”

It’s not some shadowy third-party workaround. LinktoDM uses the official Instagram API, so it’s safe, Meta-compliant, and built to scale with your account.

Still not sure?

Section titled “Still not sure?”

If you’ve ever:

  • Missed a DM that could have turned into a sale
  • Wished you could reply to everyone without losing your sanity
  • Wanted to run a giveaway without manually messaging 432 people
  • Or just felt guilty for not answering fast enough…

…LinktoDM might be exactly what you’ve been looking for.

It even got featured on ProductHunt’s top 10 of the day, so you’re not the only one impressed.

So next time someone comments “how much?”, just smile. LinktoDM’s already on it.

Go ahead. Automate like a human.

(And maybe finally take that Sunday off 😌)

title: Connect your Instagram account
html:
Connect your Instagram account

2 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Instagram login: the shortest way in

Section titled “Instagram login: the shortest way in”

Signing in with Instagram connects your account to LinktoDM directly. There’s no Facebook Page to link, no Business portfolio to pick, and no Page admin access to track down first — your Instagram credentials are the only thing you need.

That makes it the right pick for creators and small brands who want to be automating messages and building templates today rather than untangling a Facebook setup.

Take the other path, Connect your Facebook account, if you want the full feature set — Comment-to-DM, Story Replies, Click Tracking and Analytics — or if you want to automate a Facebook Page as well. A Page can even be connected on its own there, with no Instagram account involved. You can only use one of the two methods per Instagram account, so pick the one that matches what you plan to build.

Disconnect other automation tools first

Instagram grants messaging permissions to one app at a time. If ManyChat or a similar tool is still connected, your automations may silently fail, replies may arrive late, or Instagram may action-block the account. Remove those connections before you start — see Another app is controlling your conversations.

Connect with Instagram login

Section titled “Connect with Instagram login”

The whole flow takes a couple of minutes.

1. Go to console.linktodm.com

2. Pick “Continue with Instagram”

The sign-in screen offers both Facebook and Instagram. Choose Instagram to skip the Page requirement entirely.

3. Log in and approve access

Enter your Instagram credentials, then add your email ID when prompted. Approve every permission request — messaging and comment access in particular, since those are what your automations run on. LinktoDM drops you straight into the dashboard once it’s done.

title: Connect your Facebook account
html:
Connect your Facebook account

2 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Facebook login: the full automation feature set

Section titled “Facebook login: the full automation feature set”

Connecting through Facebook is the route built around a Facebook Page. The Page is what carries the messaging and comment permissions, so it’s the Page you sign in to grant — and an Instagram account is optional.

All you need is a Facebook Page you administer. Connect it on its own and LinktoDM automates the Page: Messenger DMs, and comment-to-DM on your Facebook posts. No Instagram account has to be linked for that to work.

Link an Instagram account to the Page and you get the rest — Comment-to-DM, Story Replies, Click Tracking and Analytics on Instagram. Meta only exposes those capabilities through a Page, which is why this path is the one that unlocks them. For the Instagram side you’ll also need:

  • An Instagram Business or Creator account (see Why an Instagram professional account is required).
  • That account linked to your Facebook Page (see Why a Facebook Page is required).

Either way, sign in with a Facebook account that has admin access to the Page — being able to post to it isn’t enough, and the flow won’t complete without the admin role. If you have no Page and only want to automate Instagram, Connect your Instagram account covers the lighter path.

Disconnect other automation tools first

If you’re bringing an Instagram account along, note that Instagram grants messaging permissions to one app at a time. Leave ManyChat or a similar tool connected and your automations may silently fail, replies may arrive late, or Instagram may action-block the account. Clear those connections first — see Another app is controlling your conversations.

Connect with Facebook login

Section titled “Connect with Facebook login”

1. Go to console.linktodm.com

2. Pick “Continue with Facebook”

The sign-in screen offers both Facebook and Instagram. Choose Facebook to unlock the advanced automation features.

3. Work through Meta’s permission screens

Log in with the Facebook account that administers your Page. Meta then walks you through four short screens.

title: LinktoDM plans and pricing
html:
LinktoDM plans and pricing

Updated Sep 9, 2026

LinktoDM has four plans. Free is a working plan rather than a trial: no card, no expiry, and enough of the product to run a real comment-to-DM funnel. Pro is where an automation stops being a single reply and becomes a sequence you can steer. Pro+ doesn’t add new kinds of automation so much as more room to run them — more connected accounts, more people logging in, and programmatic access. Enterprise is a quote rather than a price, for agencies managing creators as a business.

The tables below are read live from LinktoDM’s billing API when you open this page, so they can’t drift out of date the way a written-down price does. The pricing page is where you buy, and the last word if the two ever disagree.

Fetching current prices…

Live prices couldn't be loaded. See current pricing on linktodm.com.

How to read these prices

Section titled “How to read these prices”

The price shown is per month, on whichever billing cycle is selected. Yearly plans are charged once, up front, for the whole year — the toggle shows the monthly equivalent so the two cycles can be compared on the same basis, and the Billing column names the amount that actually leaves your account.

Yearly is the same product for less. There is no feature difference between the cycles; you’re buying the discount, not a different tier. Monthly makes sense while you’re still finding out whether the automations earn their keep. Yearly makes sense after a month where they did.

Tax is listed separately where it applies, because that’s how checkout presents it. An Indian subscription shows the plan price plus GST rather than one combined figure, and the total you’re charged is the two added together.

Prices are shown in your region’s currency. India is billed in rupees and everywhere else in US dollars, and the page works out which from where you’re browsing. If it can’t tell — a VPN, a privacy extension, an unusual network — it falls back to dollars and says so above the table. Currency is decided again, for real, at checkout.

What each plan is actually for

Section titled “What each plan is actually for”

Free

Section titled “Free”

Free is unusually complete, and it isn’t time-limited. You get unlimited automations, comment-to-DM, chat automation, story replies and mentions, the share trigger, the basic flow builder and your automation stats. If what you need is “someone comments a keyword, they receive a link”, Free does that indefinitely, within the DM allowance in the table above.

Where it stops is everything after that first message. There are no follow-ups, no data collection, no backtracking, no queue controls and no AI. Free delivers a message; it doesn’t build a relationship with the person who received it.

Pro

Section titled “Pro”

Two things push people from Free to Pro, and neither is usually the DM count.

The first is capture. Collecting an email address or phone number inside the DM, and exporting it, is the difference between an automation that delivered a link and one that gave you an audience you own — a list that still exists if Instagram changes its mind about your reach. Contact segmentation and personalised discount codes build on the same thing.

The second is control after something goes wrong, or right. Backtracking reaches comments that arrived before your automation existed, which matters on the post that takes off unexpectedly. Pausing or clearing the queue matters when you publish something with the wrong link in it. Both are Pro, and both are wanted at the exact moment waiting isn’t an option.

Pro also carries the pieces that turn one message into a conversation: follow-ups with conditions, opener messages, ask-to-follow, delays, AI replies and message variations.

Pro+

Section titled “Pro+”

Pro+ is about scale of operation, not capability of automation. A Pro automation and a Pro+ automation are the same automation. What changes is how many accounts run them, how many people can log in, and whether other software can drive LinktoDM on your behalf through API access. It also adds payment collection inside a flow, the AI flow builder, the AI intent trigger and AI agents that like and hide comments.

The practical test: if you’re hitting a ceiling on how many rather than what, you want Pro+. If you’re hitting a ceiling on what an automation can do, you wanted Pro and already have it.

Enterprise

Section titled “Enterprise”

Enterprise is a custom quote covering everything in Pro+ plus a creator management dashboard, unlimited creator accounts and a named contact for support and feature requests. It exists for agencies and creator networks — the case where accounts belong to clients rather than to you. Email support@linktodm.com.

Creator accounts and team members are different things

Section titled “Creator accounts and team members are different things”

These two limits get read as one, and they aren’t.

A creator account is an Instagram or Facebook account you’ve connected to LinktoDM. Each one is a separate account whose comments and DMs LinktoDM handles, and each gets its own share of Instagram’s sending limits. Running three brands means three creator accounts, even if you’re the only person who ever signs in. See adding another Instagram account for how that works.

A team member is a person with their own login to your LinktoDM workspace. Adding a colleague so they can build automations without sharing your password uses a team seat, not a creator account.

So a solo creator with four brands needs creator accounts, and a two-brand agency with six staff needs team seats. Check the table above for which plan carries enough of each — they don’t rise together, and it’s common to need one long before the other.

What “unlimited DMs” does and doesn’t cover

Section titled “What “unlimited DMs” does and doesn’t cover”

Unlimited describes LinktoDM’s side of the arrangement: the paid plans don’t meter your messages, and a month where a post performs well costs the same as a quiet one.

Instagram’s own limits are separate and apply on every plan, including Enterprise. Meta caps how fast any tool may send on your behalf — most relevantly, private replies to comments are capped per hour — and upgrading your subscription does not raise them, because they aren’t LinktoDM’s to raise. This is the ceiling most viral posts meet, not the plan.

That’s what the DM queue is for: it holds the surplus and releases it into the next window rather than discarding it, so a spike is delivered late instead of lost. DM rate limits and throttling has Meta’s published figures and explains how the queue works around each one.

The 24-hour messaging window

Instagram only allows you to message someone for 24 hours after their last interaction with you. A delay or follow-up scheduled beyond that window will fail to deliver on every plan, paid or not. It is a platform rule, not a plan limit.

How LinktoDM’s pricing compares

Section titled “How LinktoDM’s pricing compares”

Most Instagram automation tools, ManyChat included, price by contact: a low entry price for a small list that rises as the list grows. The effect is that a post which performs well raises next month’s bill, and growth costs more precisely when it’s working.

LinktoDM’s paid plans are flat, with unlimited DMs. The trade is that the ceilings sit elsewhere — on connected accounts and team seats rather than on audience size — which suits one brand sending a lot more than it suits many accounts sending little. There’s a full side-by-side on the LinktoDM vs ManyChat page, and a migration guide if you’re moving across.

Changing or cancelling your plan

Section titled “Changing or cancelling your plan”

Upgrading takes effect immediately. The usual sequence when a post is taking off mid-campaign is to upgrade, backtrack the comments you missed, and carry on in the same sitting.

Cancelling stops the next renewal rather than closing the account. The paid features keep running until the period you’ve already paid for ends, and the account then returns to Free. Your automations, contacts and connected accounts stay where they are; the steps inside them that need a paid plan simply stop running. If you’re over the Free limits at that point, that’s what to sort out before the renewal date, not after.

Purchases are not refunded, including if you cancel or delete the account part-way through a period. The refund policy is the authority on this, and it’s the main reason to test on Free before buying rather than after.

Where to start

Section titled “Where to start”

Connect one account and build one automation on Free before choosing anything. It costs nothing, takes a few minutes, and the plan question usually answers itself once you’ve seen which step you want next — a follow-up going out, or an email address coming back.

Start with Connect your Instagram account, then Create an Instagram comment-to-DM automation.

It also adds payment collection inside a flow, the AI flow builder, the AI intent trigger and AI agents that like and hide comments.

The practical test: if you’re hitting a ceiling on how many rather than what, you want Pro+. If you’re hitting a ceiling on what an automation can do, you wanted Pro and already have it.

Enterprise
Section titled “Enterprise”

Enterprise is a custom quote covering everything in Pro+ plus a creator management dashboard, unlimited creator accounts and a named contact for support and feature requests. It exists for agencies and creator networks — the case where accounts belong to clients rather than to you. Email support@linktodm.com.

Creator accounts and team members are different things
Section titled “Creator accounts and team members are different things”

These two limits get read as one, and they aren’t.

A creator account is an Instagram or Facebook account you’ve connected to LinktoDM. Each one is a separate account whose comments and DMs LinktoDM handles, and each gets its own share of Instagram’s sending limits. Running three brands means three creator accounts, even if you’re the only person who ever signs in. See adding another Instagram account for how that works.

A team member is a person with their own login to your LinktoDM workspace. Adding a colleague so they can build automations without sharing your password uses a team seat, not a creator account.

So a solo creator with four brands needs creator accounts, and a two-brand agency with six staff needs team seats. Check the table above for which plan carries enough of each — they don’t rise together, and it’s common to need one long before the other.

What “unlimited DMs” does and doesn’t cover
Section titled “What “unlimited DMs” does and doesn’t cover”

Unlimited describes LinktoDM’s side of the arrangement: the paid plans don’t meter your messages, and a month where a post performs well costs the same as a quiet one.

Instagram’s own limits are separate and apply on every plan, including Enterprise. Meta caps how fast any tool may send on your behalf — most relevantly, private replies to comments are capped per hour — and upgrading your subscription does not raise them, because they aren’t LinktoDM’s to raise. This is the ceiling most viral posts meet, not the plan.

That’s what the DM queue is for: it holds the surplus and releases it into the next window rather than discarding it, so a spike is delivered late instead of lost. DM rate limits and throttling has Meta’s published figures and explains how the queue works around each one.

The 24-hour messaging window

Instagram only allows you to message someone for 24 hours after their last interaction with you. A delay or follow-up scheduled beyond that window will fail to deliver on every plan, paid or not. It is a platform rule, not a plan limit.

How LinktoDM’s pricing compares
Section titled “How LinktoDM’s pricing compares”

Most Instagram automation tools, ManyChat included, price by contact: a low entry price for a small list that rises as the list grows. The effect is that a post which performs well raises next month’s bill, and growth costs more precisely when it’s working.

LinktoDM’s paid plans are flat, with unlimited DMs. The trade is that the ceilings sit elsewhere — on connected accounts and team seats rather than on audience size — which suits one brand sending a lot more than it suits many accounts sending little. There’s a full side-by-side on the LinktoDM vs ManyChat page, and a migration guide if you’re moving across.

Changing or cancelling your plan
Section titled “Changing or cancelling your plan”

Upgrading takes effect immediately. The usual sequence when a post is taking off mid-campaign is to upgrade, backtrack the comments you missed, and carry on in the same sitting.

Cancelling stops the next renewal rather than closing the account. The paid features keep running until the period you’ve already paid for ends, and the account then returns to Free. Your automations, contacts and connected accounts stay where they are; the steps inside them that need a paid plan simply stop running. If you’re over the Free limits at that point, that’s what to sort out before the renewal date, not after.

Purchases are not refunded, including if you cancel or delete the account part-way through a period. The refund policy is the authority on this, and it’s the main reason to test on Free before buying rather than after.

Where to start
Section titled “Where to start”

Connect one account and build one automation on Free before choosing anything. It costs nothing, takes a few minutes, and the plan question usually answers itself once you’ve seen which step you want next — a follow-up going out, or an email address coming back.

title: Create an Instagram Comment-to-DM Automation
html:
Create an Instagram Comment-to-DM Automation

4 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Imagine every time someone drops a comment on your Instagram post, they get an instant, friendly DM from you, without you even touching your phone. That’s Comment-to-DM Automation.

It’s like having a superpower where every comment turns into a private conversation, automatically. No more missed opportunities. No more forgetting to reply. Just smooth, real-time engagement that feels personal, not robotic.

Whether it’s a giveaway, a product inquiry, or a casual question, LinktoDM slides into your follower’s DMs for you, starting conversations while you’re busy running your brand (or, let’s be real, binge-watching your favorite series).

Once your Instagram account is connected to LinktoDM, you’re ready to create your first automation. Here’s exactly how to do it in just a few clicks:

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to LinktoDM
  • A published post or reel for the automation to watch
  • The DM you want to send: text, or an image with buttons

Step 1: Go to the Dashboard

Section titled “Step 1: Go to the Dashboard”

After logging in, you’ll land on the LinktoDM dashboard. This is your main control panel.

Step 2: Open Automations

Section titled “Step 2: Open Automations”

Automations is the first item in the left sidebar, and it lists everything you already have running. Above the list, All / Basic / Flow filter what you are looking at.

Step 3: Create a Post Automation

Section titled “Step 3: Create a Post Automation”

Click + New automation. The dialog offers three quick automations:

  • Post automation: replies when someone comments on a post or reel
  • Story automation: replies to story replies and reactions
  • Chat automation: replies to keywords sent in DMs

Below those sit the advanced options — Flow builder and AI assisted flow builder — plus a conversation starter and ready-made templates.

Choose Post automation for a comment-to-DM flow.

Step 4: Configure Your Automation

Section titled “Step 4: Configure Your Automation”

You’ll now walk through a few quick setup steps:

  • Select Post or Reel: Choose the content you want this automation to apply to. You’ll see three options:
    • Apply to All Posts and Reels: The automation will trigger on any post or reel, automatically.
    • Apply to Next Post or Reel: Schedule the automation for your next piece of content.
    • Apply to a Current Post or Reel: Pick an existing post or reel.
  • Set Trigger: Choose whether it should trigger on any comment, on specific keywords, or on intent match — where you describe what a comment should mean instead of listing words
  • Set Auto Reply: You can write a manual response or use LinktoDM’s AI to auto-generate replies.
  • Choose DM Type:
    • Message Template: standard text DM
    • Button Image: image with CTA buttons (up to 10 buttons)
    • Button Text: text with clickable button options
  • Enable Ask to Follow (Optional): Only send DMs if the user follows you.

Once it’s published, you can also backtrack comments — run the automation back over comments already on the post, up to 7 days old.

Step 5: Publish and Go Live

Section titled “Step 5: Publish and Go Live”

Click Publish and go live. Your automation is now running in the background, no more manual replies needed!

Pro Tip

Always test your automation by commenting from another account to make sure it’s firing correctly.

You should now have

A live post automation that watches the post you chose, replies to matching comments, and sends your DM, running whether or not you’re online.

Next: Triggers in automation

Real-World Cases and Examples

Section titled “Real-World Cases and Examples”
  • Giveaway Madness: “Comment ‘Done’ to enter!” → Auto DM bonus entry steps and watch excitement build.
  • Flash Sales: “Comment ‘SALE’ for your code!” → DM them a time-limited discount and drive FOMO.
  • Product Teasers: “Want early access? Comment ‘VIP’!” → DM secret launch info to your biggest fans.
  • Service Bookings: “Need help? Comment ‘Consult’!” → DM your booking link and get those calls lined up.
  • Event Hype: “Coming to our event? Comment ‘RSVP’!” → DM them venue details and save the date.
  • Freebies & Guides: “Want the checklist? Comment ‘Guide’!” → DM them the PDF instantly.
  • Support Made Easy: “Got an issue? Comment ‘Help’!” → DM a quick troubleshooting guide.
  • Newsletter Signups: “Stay updated! Comment ‘Subscribe’!” → DM signup link.
  • Lead Magnets: “Grab the resource! Comment ‘Download’!” → DM a freebie and collect leads.

Best Ways to Set Up

Section titled “Best Ways to Set Up”
  • Mix up your replies. Random message variations = natural convo vibes.
  • Always drop a clear CTA: “Tap the link!”, “Reply YES!”, “Claim now!”
  • Keep it on-brand: Sound like you, not a bot. Emojis? Humor? Go for it.
  • Always preview/test with a dummy account first. Nobody likes broken automations.
  • If expecting loads of comments (think big promos), let AI Auto-Reply help you out without missing a beat.

title: Choose Which Post or Reel an Automation Watches
html:
Choose Which Post or Reel an Automation Watches

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Post is the first card in the automation editor, and it answers one question: which piece of content is this automation listening to?

Nothing else runs until this is set. A trigger with no post attached has nothing to watch.

The three choices

Section titled “The three choices”

Open the dropdown on the right of the Post card:

  • A specific post or reel — pick one piece of published content from the grid. The automation only ever fires on that post.
  • Your next post or reel — arms the automation now and attaches it to the next thing you publish. Useful when the caption is written but the post isn’t live yet.
  • All posts and reels — every post and reel on the account, including ones you publish later.

Pick a specific post and a grid of your published content appears underneath. Click a thumbnail to select it; the card header updates to 1 post selected, and the live preview on the right switches to that post so you can see what your audience will be commenting on.

Which one to use

Section titled “Which one to use”

A specific post is the right default. Most automations exist for one campaign — a giveaway, a launch, a lead magnet — and the DM you write only makes sense next to that post.

Your next post saves a step when you’re publishing on a schedule. Set the automation up in the morning, publish at 6pm, and the automation attaches itself.

All posts and reels is a standing net rather than a campaign. It suits one broad, evergreen automation — “comment anything and I’ll send you the link in bio” — and it does not suit keyword campaigns, because the same DM would go out on every post you publish for the rest of the year.

One post, one automation

Two live automations watching the same post both fire, and a commenter gets two DMs. If you want different keywords to send different DMs on one post, use multiple keywords in a single automation or build it in the Flow builder instead of publishing two.

Changing the post later

Section titled “Changing the post later”

The selection is not locked once you publish. Reopen the automation, click the Post card, and choose different content — the trigger, replies and DM all stay as they were. This is the quick way to reuse a campaign that worked: point last month’s automation at this month’s post rather than rebuilding it.

Reels, image posts and carousels all work the same way. Stories do not appear here — those belong to a story automation, which is a separate type.

title: Instagram Automation Triggers
html:
Instagram Automation Triggers

Updated Sep 9, 2026

When it comes to setting up your Instagram DM automations inside LinktoDM, Triggers are where the magic begins.

Triggers tell LinktoDM when to jump into action, whether it’s replying to a comment, reacting to a story, or sliding into someone’s DMs at just the right moment.

And don’t worry, setting them up is ridiculously easy.

You get three trigger choices for both Post/Reel Automations and Story Reaction Automations. Two of them match on words; the third matches on meaning.

1: Any Word Trigger

Section titled “1: Any Word Trigger”

If you want to keep it simple and respond to any comment or any story reaction, this is your go-to.

When you choose “Any Word” trigger, LinktoDM will send out your preset DM the moment someone comments anything on your selected post or reel, or reacts to your story, no matter what emoji they tap.

Perfect for:

  • Building engagement on reels
  • Running Instagram giveaways (Example: “Comment anything to enter!”)
  • Turning casual story reactions into meaningful DMs

Real Example

Someone comments “Love this 🥰” on your new product reel → LinktoDM immediately DMs them a thank-you message plus a special offer link.

2: Specific Word Trigger

Section titled “2: Specific Word Trigger”

Want to be a little more selective about who gets a DM? Specific Word Trigger has your back.

Here, LinktoDM sends your automation only if a comment includes a keyword you define. No keyword, no DM.

Perfect for:

  • Gathering qualified leads (“Comment INFO to get more details!”)
  • Running secret giveaways (“Only those who comment VIP get the special code!”)
  • Saving time by filtering out general chatter

Real Example

You set “price” as the trigger word. Someone comments “What’s the price for this?” → LinktoDM sends them an instant DM with the product pricing and checkout link.

Type a keyword into Add keyword and press Enter. Each one becomes a chip you can remove with its ×, and a comment matching any of them fires the automation — they’re alternatives, not a phrase the comment has to contain in full.

Matching ignores case and finds the keyword inside a longer sentence, so price catches “Price?”, “what’s the PRICE” and “pricing please” alike.

3: Intent Match

Section titled “3: Intent Match”

Keywords only fire when someone uses your word. Real comment sections don’t cooperate: the same question arrives as “How much?”, “Cost?”, “price pls” and “Discount milega kya?”, and a keyword list never covers all of it.

Intent Match flips the problem around. Instead of listing words, you describe what a comment has to mean, and every comment on that post is checked against your description.

Pick it from the trigger dropdown on the right of the Trigger card.

Describing the intent

Section titled “Describing the intent”

The card turns into a single question: What should the comment mean?

Write it the way you’d explain it to a teammate — one plain sentence, up to 300 characters. No keyword lists, no syntax.

  • Looking for the price of the product.
  • Looking for where to purchase the product.
  • Looking for a discount or promotional offer.
  • Looking for information about product availability.

You can also cover several intents in one line — Looking for the price, discount, or purchase information. — when a single automation should answer all of them.

Hit Validate prompt to have LinktoDM check the description reads clearly before you publish.

What it catches

Section titled “What it catches”

With Looking for the price of the product. set, all of these fire the automation, even though none of them contain the word “price”:

  • “How much?”
  • “Cost?”
  • “How much is it”

And with Looking for where to purchase the product., so do “Where can I get this?”, “How do I get my hands on one?” and a bare “Where?”.

It reads Hinglish and Manglish too

Intent Match works on meaning, not on English spelling, so romanised Indian-language comments are matched like any other. In testing, “Discount milega kya?” triggered a Looking for a discount or promotional offer. automation and got the discount reply — no keyword, no English, still matched.

If your audience comments in Hinglish, Manglish, Tanglish or any other mixed script, this is the trigger to use. Write your description in plain English; you don’t need to list the local phrasings.

What it leaves alone

Section titled “What it leaves alone”

Just as important: comments that don’t match your description are skipped. With Looking for the price, discount, or purchase information. set, “What material is it made of?” and “I love this product” sat in the comment section untouched while the price and offer questions got replies.

That boundary is what makes Intent Match safe to leave running on a busy post — a broad description doesn’t mean a DM to everyone who comments.

It’s a description, not a command

The field describes the commenter’s intent, not what you want to happen. Write “Looking for the price of the product”, not “Send them the price”. Descriptions phrased as instructions match unpredictably.

When to use which

Section titled “When to use which”
You want to… Use
DM everyone who comments or reacts Any Word
DM only people who type your exact campaign word Specific Word
DM everyone asking a kind of question, however they word it Intent Match

Intent Match is the one to reach for on evergreen product posts, where the same handful of questions come in endlessly in different words. Keep Specific Word for campaigns where the keyword is part of the call to action — “Comment VIP” only works if VIP is what you’re matching.

Two toggles worth knowing

Section titled “Two toggles worth knowing”

Both sit under the trigger’s settings — whichever trigger type you picked — and both are off by default.

Trigger for share media

Section titled “Trigger for share media”

Labelled Also trigger on shares in the Intent Match card. Fires the automation when someone shares your post into their DMs with you, not just when they comment on it. Shares are a quieter, higher-intent signal than a public comment — the person is already in your inbox — so this is worth turning on for lead magnets and product posts.

One DM per user

Section titled “One DM per user”

Sends one DM per person within a time window, no matter how many times they comment. Without it, someone who comments “link” three times gets three DMs.

Turn this on for anything running at scale — giveaways especially, where people comment repeatedly to boost their odds. It protects both your send volume and the recipient’s inbox.

Best Practices for Using Triggers

Section titled “Best Practices for Using Triggers”

Here’s how the pros use triggers without getting shadowbanned or spamming their audience:

  • For mass engagement (giveaways, launches): Stick to Any Word Trigger. Cast a wide net.
  • For targeted marketing (sales, lead gen): Use Specific Word Trigger to only engage hot prospects.
  • For real questions in a real comment section: Use Intent Match, especially where people comment in Hinglish, Manglish or a mix of scripts.
  • Always test your trigger before going live. (Seriously, drop a comment from your second account or have a friend help. Better safe than confused.)
  • Use simple keywords for specific triggers. Words like “info,” “price,” “book” are perfect. No long phrases.
  • Keep intent descriptions narrow. One intent per automation reads more reliably than a description trying to cover five. Split them across automations, or list them explicitly in one line.
  • For Story Automation: “Any Word” works best because most story replies are just emojis or quick one-word reactions.
  • Keep your tone casual inside your auto-replies. Instagram is a relaxed platform. You don’t want your DM to feel like a formal email from 1999.
  • Don’t over-trigger. Set reasonable limits inside LinktoDM to keep your comment section and account healthy.

text:
Instagram Automation Triggers

Updated Sep 9, 2026

When it comes to setting up your Instagram DM automations inside LinktoDM, Triggers are where the magic begins.

Triggers tell LinktoDM when to jump into action, whether it’s replying to a comment, reacting to a story, or sliding into someone’s DMs at just the right moment.

And don’t worry, setting them up is ridiculously easy.

You get three trigger choices for both Post/Reel Automations and Story Reaction Automations. Two of them match on words; the third matches on meaning.

1: Any Word Trigger
Section titled “1: Any Word Trigger”

If you want to keep it simple and respond to any comment or any story reaction, this is your go-to.

When you choose “Any Word” trigger, LinktoDM will send out your preset DM the moment someone comments anything on your selected post or reel, or reacts to your story, no matter what emoji they tap.

Perfect for:

Building engagement on reels
Running Instagram giveaways (Example: “Comment anything to enter!”)
Turning casual story reactions into meaningful DMs

Real Example

Someone comments “Love this 🥰” on your new product reel → LinktoDM immediately DMs them a thank-you message plus a special offer link.

The same trigger in the Flow builder, where it is called Any message
2: Specific Word Trigger
Section titled “2: Specific Word Trigger”

Want to be a little more selective about who gets a DM? Specific Word Trigger has your back.

Here, LinktoDM sends your automation only if a comment includes a keyword you define. No keyword, no DM.

Perfect for:

Gathering qualified leads (“Comment INFO to get more details!”)
Running secret giveaways (“Only those who comment VIP get the special code!”)
Saving time by filtering out general chatter

Real Example

You set “price” as the trigger word. Someone comments “What’s the price for this?” → LinktoDM sends them an instant DM with the product pricing and checkout link.

Type a keyword into Add keyword and press Enter. Each one becomes a chip you can remove with its ×, and a comment matching any of them fires the automation — they’re alternatives, not a phrase the comment has to contain in full.

Matching ignores case and finds the keyword inside a longer sentence, so price catches “Price?”, “what’s the PRICE” and “pricing please” alike.

Keywords are chips; the two toggles below widen and narrow what counts as a trigger
3: Intent Match
Section titled “3: Intent Match”

Keywords only fire when someone uses your word. Real comment sections don’t cooperate: the same question arrives as “How much?”, “Cost?”, “price pls” and “Discount milega kya?”, and a keyword list never covers all of it.

Intent Match flips the problem around. Instead of listing words, you describe what a comment has to mean, and every comment on that post is checked against your description.

Pick it from the trigger dropdown on the right of the Trigger card.

Intent match sits alongside the two keyword options in the same dropdown
Describing the intent
Section titled “Describing the intent”

The card turns into a single question: What should the comment mean?

Write it the way you’d explain it to a teammate — one plain sentence, up to 300 characters. No keyword lists, no syntax.

Looking for the price of the product.
Looking for where to purchase the product.
Looking for a discount or promotional offer.
Looking for information about product availability.

You can also cover several intents in one line — Looking for the price, discount, or purchase information. — when a single automation should answer all of them.

Hit Validate prompt to have LinktoDM check the description reads clearly before you publish.

One sentence replaces the keyword list — the counter caps you at 300 characters
What it catches
Section titled “What it catches”

With Looking for the price of the product. set, all of these fire the automation, even though none of them contain the word “price”:

“How much?”
“Cost?”
“How much is it”

And with Looking for where to purchase the product., so do “Where can I get this?”, “How do I get my hands on one?” and a bare “Where?”.

It reads Hinglish and Manglish too

Intent Match works on meaning, not on English spelling, so romanised Indian-language comments are matched like any other. In testing, “Discount milega kya?” triggered a Looking for a discount or promotional offer. automation and got the discount reply — no keyword, no English, still matched.

If your audience comments in Hinglish, Manglish, Tanglish or any other mixed script, this is the trigger to use. Write your description in plain English; you don’t need to list the local phrasings.

What it leaves alone
Section titled “What it leaves alone”

Just as important: comments that don’t match your description are skipped. With Looking for the price, discount, or purchase information. set, “What material is it made of?” and “I love this product” sat in the comment section untouched while the price and offer questions got replies.

That boundary is what makes Intent Match safe to leave running on a busy post — a broad description doesn’t mean a DM to everyone who comments.

It’s a description, not a command

The field describes the commenter’s intent, not what you want to happen. Write “Looking for the price of the product”, not “Send them the price”. Descriptions phrased as instructions match unpredictably.

When to use which
Section titled “When to use which”
YOU WANT TO…	USE
DM everyone who comments or reacts	Any Word
DM only people who type your exact campaign word	Specific Word
DM everyone asking a kind of question, however they word it	Intent Match

Intent Match is the one to reach for on evergreen product posts, where the same handful of questions come in endlessly in different words. Keep Specific Word for campaigns where the keyword is part of the call to action — “Comment VIP” only works if VIP is what you’re matching.

Two toggles worth knowing
Section titled “Two toggles worth knowing”

Both sit under the trigger’s settings — whichever trigger type you picked — and both are off by default.

Trigger for share media
Section titled “Trigger for share media”

Labelled Also trigger on shares in the Intent Match card. Fires the automation when someone shares your post into their DMs with you, not just when they comment on it. Shares are a quieter, higher-intent signal than a public comment — the person is already in your inbox — so this is worth turning on for lead magnets and product posts.

One DM per user
Section titled “One DM per user”

Sends one DM per person within a time window, no matter how many times they comment. Without it, someone who comments “link” three times gets three DMs.

Turn this on for anything running at scale — giveaways especially, where people comment repeatedly to boost their odds. It protects both your send volume and the recipient’s inbox.

Best Practices for Using Triggers
Section titled “Best Practices for Using Triggers”

Here’s how the pros use triggers without getting shadowbanned or spamming their audience:

For mass engagement (giveaways, launches): Stick to Any Word Trigger. Cast a wide net.
For targeted marketing (sales, lead gen): Use Specific Word Trigger to only engage hot prospects.
For real questions in a real comment section: Use Intent Match, especially where people comment in Hinglish, Manglish or a mix of scripts.
Always test your trigger before going live. (Seriously, drop a comment from your second account or have a friend help. Better safe than confused.)
Use simple keywords for specific triggers. Words like “info,” “price,” “book” are perfect. No long phrases.
Keep intent descriptions narrow. One intent per automation reads more reliably than a description trying to cover five. Split them across automations, or list them explicitly in one line.
For Story Automation: “Any Word” works best because most story replies are just emojis or quick one-word reactions.
Keep your tone casual inside your auto-replies. Instagram is a relaxed platform. You don’t want your DM to feel like a formal email from 1999.
Don’t over-trigger. Set reasonable limits inside LinktoDM to keep your comment section and account healthy.

title: Public Comment Replies You Write Yourself
html:
Public Comment Replies You Write Yourself

Updated Sep 9, 2026

When your automation fires, it does two things: it sends the DM, and — if you let it — it leaves a public reply under the comment that triggered it.

The public reply is the part everyone else scrolling the post can see. It tells the commenter to go and check their inbox, and it tells everyone else that commenting gets a response.

Turning it on

Section titled “Turning it on”

The Public comment reply card has a toggle on its right. Off, the automation still sends DMs — it just stays out of your comment section.

Switch it on and choose Manual to write the replies yourself. (The other tab, AI, generates a fresh reply for every comment from a prompt.)

Writing the replies

Section titled “Writing the replies”

Type a reply and press Enter. It joins the list above the field, with a bin icon to delete it. Add as many as you like.

Insert {{username}} to drop the commenter’s Instagram handle into the reply — there’s a shortcut button on the right of the input. “Sent it over, {{username}} 💌” reads like you typed it; “Sent it over” repeated forty times does not.

Add three or more

Section titled “Add three or more”

LinktoDM prompts you for at least three replies, and the reason is visible from the outside: a comment section where every reply is the identical sentence is the clearest possible signal that a bot is running the account.

With more than one reply saved, Rotate randomly per comment picks a different one each time, so the section reads like a person answering rather than a script.

Three or four short variants is plenty:

  • “Just sent it 📩”
  • “Check your DMs, {{username}}!”
  • “On its way — have a look at your message requests too”
  • “Sent! Let me know if it doesn’t land”

Limit how many go out

Section titled “Limit how many go out”

The dropdown in the card header caps public replies per post — limit to 100 per post by default. The DM automation keeps running after the cap; only the public replies stop.

This matters on a post that takes off. A hundred replies from your account under one post is engagement; a thousand is a wall of your own name, and Instagram’s spam systems notice. If you want the reasoning and the numbers, see Limit public replies.

Pro Tip

Mention the message request folder in at least one variant. First-time DMs from an account someone doesn’t follow often land there, and “check your requests” is the difference between a delivered DM and an unread one.

title: AI Public Comment Replies
html:
AI Public Comment Replies

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Writing four public replies by hand is fine. Writing enough of them that a busy post never repeats itself is not — which is where the AI tab comes in.

Instead of a list of replies, you give LinktoDM a prompt. Every comment that fires the automation gets its own reply, written on the spot from that prompt and the comment it’s answering.

Setting it up

Section titled “Setting it up”

In the Public comment reply card, switch the toggle on and pick AI — it’s the recommended tab.

Writing the prompt

Section titled “Writing the prompt”

The prompt is a description of what the reply should do and how it should sound, not the reply itself. The default is a good shape to copy:

Thank {{username}} for commenting and let them know a special link is waiting in their DMs, with a friendly, cheerful tone.

Three things make a prompt work:

  • The job. Point them to their DMs, thank them, answer the question — say which.
  • The tone. “Friendly and cheerful”, “short and dry”, “warm, no emojis”. The AI will otherwise default to a brightness that may not be yours.
  • {{username}} where you want the commenter’s handle.

You have 400 characters, and the counter under the box tracks them.

Regenerate prompt rewrites the prompt itself — useful when you know roughly what you want but not how to phrase it. Show preview renders sample replies so you can hear the tone before anyone else does.

AI or manual?

Section titled “AI or manual?”

Use AI when comment volume is high or unpredictable, when comments are actual questions rather than a keyword, or when you want the section to look genuinely conversational.

Use manual when the reply must be exact — a legal phrase, a promo code, a specific instruction — or when you’d rather approve every sentence your account posts in public.

Preview before publishing

The AI writes in public, under your name, at comment speed. Run Show preview and read a few samples first — a prompt that’s slightly off produces dozens of slightly-off replies before you notice.

The per-post cap in the card header applies here exactly as it does to manual replies: once it’s reached, public replies stop and DMs carry on.

title: DM Message Layouts: Plain Text, Buttons and Attachments
html:
DM Message Layouts: Plain Text, Buttons and Attachments

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The Message card is the DM itself. The dropdown in its header decides what shape that DM takes — and the shape matters more than most people expect, because a tappable button gets clicked far more often than a link pasted into a sentence.

Plain text

Section titled “Plain text”

Just words. Up to 900 characters, links included.

Instagram turns a pasted URL into a tappable link, so plain text is perfectly workable for a single link — it just looks like a normal message rather than a card. Use it for conversational openers, answers to questions, and anywhere a designed card would feel like an ad.

Text with button

Section titled “Text with button”

The same message, with up to three buttons underneath it. Each button has a link and a label of up to 20 characters.

This is the workhorse for link campaigns. The message explains, the button gets tapped, and you get a click you can count. + Add link adds a second and third button — enough for “Shop now / See sizes / Talk to us” without turning the DM into a menu.

Note the message allowance drops to 620 characters here to leave room for the buttons.

Image with button

Section titled “Image with button”

A card: image on top, title, and buttons under it. Add more cards and they send as a swipeable carousel — up to ten.

This is the layout for products, tiers, or anything with more than one option. It’s covered in full, with the sizes and limits, in Media in DMs.

Attachment

Section titled “Attachment”

Sends a file — image, video, GIF, audio or PDF — instead of a formatted message. Also in Media in DMs.

Choosing

Section titled “Choosing”
You want to… Use
Answer a question, sound human Plain text
Send one link and count the taps Text with button
Show a product, or several Image with button
Deliver a guide, price list or clip Attachment

Pro Tip

Switching layout keeps the text you’ve already written where it can carry over, so it’s cheap to try one against another. Watch the live preview on the right as you switch — it renders the DM exactly as it lands in someone’s inbox.

Every layout can be rotated through variations, so picking a card layout doesn’t mean sending an identical card to everyone.

title: Send Images, Video, GIFs and Carousels in a DM
html:
Send Images, Video, GIFs and Carousels in a DM

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Two of the four message layouts send media rather than text: image with button builds a card, and attachment sends a file.

Image cards and carousels

Section titled “Image cards and carousels”

Pick image with button and the Message card turns into a card editor with a live preview beside it.

Each card holds:

  • Card image — upload a file, or use the cover frame of a reel
  • Link — where the button goes
  • Title — up to 80 characters, shown under the image
  • Button label — up to 20 characters
  • + Add link — up to three buttons on the card

+ Add another card adds a second, up to ten in total, and anything past the first sends as a swipeable carousel.

A carousel is the right call when the reader has a choice to make — three products, three price tiers, three services. It’s the wrong call when there’s one action you want taken, because a swipeable row invites browsing instead of tapping.

Pro Tip

Put the option most people want in card one. Carousel analytics across messaging apps say the same thing every time: the first card takes the overwhelming majority of taps.

Attachments

Section titled “Attachments”

Pick attachment and you get an upload box: drop a file in, click Upload file, Record audio for a voice note, or Pick recent to reuse something you’ve already sent.

What you can send

Section titled “What you can send”
Type Formats Limit
Image PNG, JPG, GIF 8 MB
Video MP4, MOV 25 MB
Audio AAC, M4A, WAV 25 MB
Document PDF 25 MB

GIFs go through as images — an 8 MB ceiling, which most short loops fit under comfortably, but a long screen recording exported as a GIF will not. Export it as MP4 instead and it gets the 25 MB video allowance.

Using them well

Section titled “Using them well”
  • PDFs deliver the lead magnet directly, instead of sending someone to a landing page to download it. Fewer steps, fewer drop-offs.
  • Video works for demos and unboxings, where showing beats describing.
  • Voice notes are unusually effective for high-touch services — a fifteen second “hey, thanks for commenting” in your actual voice reads as personal in a way no text can.

Attachments send on their own

An attachment is the whole message — there’s no caption field alongside it. If the file needs context, add an opener message before it — that one does take text and a button.

Both media layouts support variations, so the file or card can differ between recipients.

Title — up to 80 characters, shown under the image
Button label — up to 20 characters
+ Add link — up to three buttons on the card

+ Add another card adds a second, up to ten in total, and anything past the first sends as a swipeable carousel.

A carousel is the right call when the reader has a choice to make — three products, three price tiers, three services. It’s the wrong call when there’s one action you want taken, because a swipeable row invites browsing instead of tapping.

Pro Tip

Put the option most people want in card one. Carousel analytics across messaging apps say the same thing every time: the first card takes the overwhelming majority of taps.

Attachments
Section titled “Attachments”

Pick attachment and you get an upload box: drop a file in, click Upload file, Record audio for a voice note, or Pick recent to reuse something you’ve already sent.

The upload box lists what Instagram will accept, with the limits
What you can send
Section titled “What you can send”
TYPE	FORMATS	LIMIT
Image	PNG, JPG, GIF	8 MB
Video	MP4, MOV	25 MB
Audio	AAC, M4A, WAV	25 MB
Document	PDF	25 MB

GIFs go through as images — an 8 MB ceiling, which most short loops fit under comfortably, but a long screen recording exported as a GIF will not. Export it as MP4 instead and it gets the 25 MB video allowance.

Using them well
Section titled “Using them well”
PDFs deliver the lead magnet directly, instead of sending someone to a landing page to download it. Fewer steps, fewer drop-offs.
Video works for demos and unboxings, where showing beats describing.
Voice notes are unusually effective for high-touch services — a fifteen second “hey, thanks for commenting” in your actual voice reads as personal in a way no text can.

Attachments send on their own

An attachment is the whole message — there’s no caption field alongside it. If the file needs context, add an opener message before it — that one does take text and a button.

Both media layouts support variations, so the file or card can differ between recipients.

title: Message Variations: Stop Every DM Reading the Same
html:
Message Variations: Stop Every DM Reading the Same

Updated Sep 9, 2026

An automation that sends one message sends it perfectly, identically, every time. That’s the problem. A hundred people receiving a character-for-character identical DM is the most legible bot signal there is — to the people reading it, and to the platform delivering it.

Variations are alternate wordings of the same DM. LinktoDM rotates them automatically, so the message stays yours and no two recipients get quite the same one.

Adding them

Section titled “Adding them”

The Variations strip sits at the top of the Message card, above the text. Click Add variations — or Edit variations (5) once some exist.

The dialog opens with your message as the starting point and generates alternates from it.

Each variation has its own box, a regenerate icon to rewrite just that one, and a bin to delete it. Regenerate at the top rewrites the whole set. Edit any of them by typing — they’re normal text fields, and the AI’s suggestion is a starting point rather than the finished copy. Save when you’re happy.

How many

Section titled “How many”

Five is the practical target and what the dialog generates by default. Below three, the rotation is noticeable to anyone who compares notes; above five, you’re maintaining copy nobody will read closely.

What to vary

Section titled “What to vary”

Vary the wrapper, not the payload.

The link, the offer, the discount code and the instruction have to be identical in every variation — that’s the thing you’re actually sending. What changes is the sentence around it:

  • “Here’s the link: …”
  • “Check this out: …”
  • “As promised 👇 …”
  • “Link’s right here: …”
  • “Sending it over now — …”

Keep them the same length and register. A set where one variation is a chirpy two-liner and another is a formal paragraph doesn’t read as natural variety, it reads as two different people.

Check every variation before you publish

Variations rotate without further review, so a typo or a broken link in variation four goes out to a fifth of your recipients and won’t show up in your own test. Read all of them.

Where else they apply

Section titled “Where else they apply”

Variations exist on every message layout — plain text, text with button, image cards and attachments — so a carousel campaign can rotate its wording too.

The same principle drives multiple public replies in your comment section, and the Randomizer node in the Flow builder, which splits people down different paths rather than just rewording one message.

title: Add a Delay Between Automation Steps
html:
Add a Delay Between Automation Steps

Updated Sep 9, 2026

An instant reply is the one thing no human has ever sent. Someone comments, and half a second later a perfectly formatted DM arrives — the timing alone gives it away.

Delay puts a pause between two steps.

Turning delays on

Section titled “Turning delays on”

Enable delay at the top right of the editor switches the feature on for the whole automation. Small Add delay buttons then appear between the cards: between the trigger and the public reply, between the public reply and the DM, and between every step in the DM sequence.

Click one and set the wait.

The delay shows in the timeline once added, and clicking it again lets you change or remove it. Each is independent, so a sequence can wait ten seconds before the DM and two days before the follow-up.

How long

Section titled “How long”

Seconds are for realism. Five to fifteen seconds before the first DM is the sweet spot: long enough not to look instant, short enough that the person is still holding their phone. This is the delay to add if you only add one.

Minutes space out a multi-message sequence so it doesn’t land as a wall of notifications.

Hours and days are for coming back later — a reminder, a second chance at an offer, a nudge to someone who never replied. Nobody thinks a two-day gap is a human typing; that’s not what it’s for.

Instagram’s 24-hour window

Instagram only lets you message someone freely for 24 hours after their last interaction with you. A delay that pushes a message past that window can stop it being delivered at all. Keep automated follow-ups inside a day of the comment that started the conversation.

Where delays earn their keep

Section titled “Where delays earn their keep”
  • Before the first DM — ten seconds, so the reply doesn’t read as automated
  • Between DM steps — thirty seconds, so a three-part message doesn’t arrive as one buzz
  • Before asking for an email — give the value first, then ask; a request that lands simultaneously with the offer feels like a toll gate
  • Before a follow-up — hours, not seconds

The Delay node does the same job in the Flow builder, with the same units.

title: Opener Message: Get a Tap Before You Send the Link
html:
Opener Message: Get a Tap Before You Send the Link

Updated Sep 9, 2026

An opener message is a short greeting with a button, sent before the message that actually carries your link.

It looks like a wasted step. It isn’t — it’s the step that gets your link opened.

Why it works

Section titled “Why it works”

A first DM to someone who doesn’t follow you often lands in message requests, where it sits unread. The moment that person taps anything — including a button in your message — they’ve interacted, and the thread behaves like a normal conversation from then on.

So the opener trades one tap for a delivered link. It also filters: someone who taps Get the link is actually interested, which makes every number downstream mean something.

Setting it up

Section titled “Setting it up”

Click Opener message in the row of step buttons at the bottom of the DM section. It’s added above your main message.

Fill in:

  • Message — up to 640 characters. Use {{username}} for the recipient’s handle.
  • Button label — up to 20 characters.
  • When tapped — Continue to next step, which runs the rest of your DM sequence.

The preview beside the fields shows the message as it will arrive, and the live preview on the right shows it in the thread.

Writing one

Section titled “Writing one”

Keep it to one or two lines. The opener’s whole job is earning a tap, so anything that isn’t working towards the tap is in the way.

  • Greet them by name. Hey {{username}}! — it’s their handle, and it proves a human set this up.
  • Say what the button does. “Get the link”, “Send me the guide”, “Show me the code”. Never “Click here” — the label is the promise.
  • Don’t explain the offer yet. That’s the next message’s job.

A working opener:

Hey {{username}}! So glad you commented 😊 Tap below and I’ll send that link straight over.

Pro Tip

Put a delay of five to ten seconds before the opener. An instant greeting the moment someone comments is the tell-tale sign of automation; a few seconds reads as you noticing.

Opener, or ask to follow?

Section titled “Opener, or ask to follow?”

They’re different asks and they stack in this order:

  1. Opener message — get a tap, warm up the thread
  2. Ask to follow — require a follow before the DM goes out
  3. Collect email — ask for contact details
  4. Message — deliver what you promised

Each one adds friction. Adding all four to a giveaway will cost you entrants — pick the ones whose value you’d defend out loud.

title: Ask to Follow Before Sending the DM
html:
Ask to Follow Before Sending the DM

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Ask to follow to receive DM holds the message back until the recipient follows you. It’s the follow-for-value trade, run automatically: they wanted the link, the link costs a follow.

The two steps

Section titled “The two steps”

Add it from the step buttons under the DM section. It arrives as a two-step sequence, and both halves are already written.

Step 1 · Ask sends the ask message with one button — Yes, I’m following. Tapping it makes LinktoDM check whether they actually follow you. If they do, the sequence continues and the DM is delivered.

Step 2 · Nudge runs only if the check fails. It sends the nudge message with two buttons: Visit my profile, which opens your profile so they can follow, and Yes, I followed, which re-checks and sends the DM.

The check is real. Tapping Yes, I’m following without following does not get anyone the message — it gets them the nudge.

Editing the copy

Section titled “Editing the copy”

Both messages are yours to rewrite, up to 620 characters each, and each button label up to 20. What you can’t change is the wiring: button one on step 1 checks, button one on step 2 opens your profile, button two on step 2 re-checks and sends.

Keep the ask light. The defaults get the tone right:

Just checking… are you already following us so we can send the message?

That framing assumes good faith — most people commenting on your post do follow you — instead of accusing anyone of freeloading. The nudge can be warmer still:

Oops 😅 You’re not following yet! Please follow us so we can send your message.

When to use it — and when not to

Section titled “When to use it — and when not to”

Worth it for giveaways, exclusive drops, and any lead magnet where “follow to enter” was already the deal you announced in the caption.

Not worth it for customer support, order questions, or anything a paying customer asked for. Making someone follow you before you’ll answer their question about a delivery is the fastest way to turn a customer into an ex-one.

It will cost you conversions

Every gate loses people. Some proportion of your commenters will read the ask, decide the link isn’t worth a follow, and leave. That’s the trade — a smaller number of more committed followers. Make sure the thing behind the gate is worth it, and say what it is in the ask.

Ordering it

Section titled “Ordering it”

Ask to follow sits after the opener message and before collecting contact details. One gate is usually plenty — asking for a follow and an email and a phone number before delivering a free checklist is three chances to be told no.

title: Collect an Email or Phone Number in the DM
html:
Collect an Email or Phone Number in the DM

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A DM conversation is a lead you can only reach on one platform. Collect email and Collect phone turn it into one you own — asked for in the thread, validated on the spot, and saved to Contacts.

Both are added from Collect info in the row of step buttons.

Collect email

Section titled “Collect email”

Ask message is the question — up to 900 characters, though a single line is what works.

Retry message is what they get when their reply isn’t a valid email address. The automation waits and asks again rather than moving on, so a typo doesn’t cost you the lead.

Collect phone

Section titled “Collect phone”

Identical in structure, with one thing to get right: ask for the country code, and show an example. The default retry does exactly that:

Oops! Please enter a valid phone number including country code e.g. +91 9496537130

Without a country code a number is ambiguous and often unusable. Putting a formatted example in both the ask and the retry saves most of the failures.

Where the answers go

Section titled “Where the answers go”

Valid replies save to Contacts, against the profile that sent them, ready to export or sync to your email or SMS tool. Nothing is lost if someone drops out mid-sequence — whatever they’d already given is kept.

Asking well

Section titled “Asking well”
  • Give first, ask second. Put the collect step after they’ve received something, or at minimum after the opener. Asking for an email before you’ve delivered anything is a form nobody filled in.
  • Say why. “Where should I send the guide?” outperforms “Enter your email” — the first is a delivery question, the second is a data request.
  • Ask for one thing. Email or phone. Both, back to back, reads as a signup form and gets abandoned like one.
  • Match the channel to the follow-up. Only collect a phone number if you genuinely intend to text or call. Collecting it because the field exists builds a list you’ll never use and a permission you didn’t need.

Consent isn’t implied

Someone answering “what’s your email?” in a DM has not opted into a marketing list. If the address is going into a newsletter, say so in the ask — and keep whatever your local rules (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, and the rest) require you to keep.

Ordering it

Section titled “Ordering it”

Collect steps come last, after the opener message and any ask to follow, and before the message that delivers what you promised — so the exchange is a fair one: they give you an address, and the thing they wanted arrives right after.

text:
Collect an Email or Phone Number in the DM

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A DM conversation is a lead you can only reach on one platform. Collect email and Collect phone turn it into one you own — asked for in the thread, validated on the spot, and saved to Contacts.

Both are added from Collect info in the row of step buttons.

Collect email
Section titled “Collect email”
Ask, validate, retry — the preview shows both the good path and the invalid one

Ask message is the question — up to 900 characters, though a single line is what works.

Retry message is what they get when their reply isn’t a valid email address. The automation waits and asks again rather than moving on, so a typo doesn’t cost you the lead.

Collect phone
Section titled “Collect phone”
Same shape, stricter validation — the retry message should show the format you want

Identical in structure, with one thing to get right: ask for the country code, and show an example. The default retry does exactly that:

Oops! Please enter a valid phone number including country code e.g. +91 9496537130

Without a country code a number is ambiguous and often unusable. Putting a formatted example in both the ask and the retry saves most of the failures.

Where the answers go
Section titled “Where the answers go”

Valid replies save to Contacts, against the profile that sent them, ready to export or sync to your email or SMS tool. Nothing is lost if someone drops out mid-sequence — whatever they’d already given is kept.

Asking well
Section titled “Asking well”
Give first, ask second. Put the collect step after they’ve received something, or at minimum after the opener. Asking for an email before you’ve delivered anything is a form nobody filled in.
Say why. “Where should I send the guide?” outperforms “Enter your email” — the first is a delivery question, the second is a data request.
Ask for one thing. Email or phone. Both, back to back, reads as a signup form and gets abandoned like one.
Match the channel to the follow-up. Only collect a phone number if you genuinely intend to text or call. Collecting it because the field exists builds a list you’ll never use and a permission you didn’t need.

Consent isn’t implied

Someone answering “what’s your email?” in a DM has not opted into a marketing list. If the address is going into a newsletter, say so in the ask — and keep whatever your local rules (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, and the rest) require you to keep.

Ordering it
Section titled “Ordering it”

Collect steps come last, after the opener message and any ask to follow, and before the message that delivers what you promised — so the exchange is a fair one: they give you an address, and the thing they wanted arrives right after.

title: Follow-Up Messages and When They Send
html:
Follow-Up Messages and When They Send

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Most people who receive your DM won’t act on it the first time. They’re mid-scroll, the link gets read later, later never arrives.

A follow-up message is the second attempt — and because you can attach a condition to it, it goes only to the people who need it.

Adding one

Section titled “Adding one”

Click Follow up message in the row of step buttons at the bottom of the DM section. Write the message the same way as any other — plain text, buttons, an attachment — then pick the condition that decides who receives it.

The conditions

Section titled “The conditions”

Always sends to everyone who reached this point, no condition applied.

Message

Section titled “Message”
  • Seen message — they opened the DM
  • Not seen message — they didn’t
  • Reacted with emoji — they tapped a reaction on it

Link

Section titled “Link”
  • Clicked the link — they tapped through
  • Didn’t click the link — they didn’t

Follow

Section titled “Follow”
  • Followed you — they followed after the DM
  • Unfollowed you — they left

Choosing the right one

Section titled “Choosing the right one”

The condition is what separates a useful nudge from a message people mute you over. Match it to what you actually want to happen next.

Not seen message is the safest and usually the most valuable. These people never saw the first DM at all — very often it’s sitting in message requests. A follow-up here isn’t a repeat, it’s a first delivery.

Didn’t click the link is the conversion nudge. They read it and didn’t act, so the second message should give a different reason rather than repeat the first — a deadline, an objection answered, a shorter ask.

Clicked the link is the one people forget, and it’s the warmest audience you have. They’re interested. Follow up with the next step: a question, a discount, a booking link.

Reacted with emoji is a reply without words. A 🔥 on a product DM is permission to keep talking.

Followed you pairs naturally with ask to follow — thank them, or deliver the thing the follow unlocked.

Unfollowed you should almost always be left alone. Someone who just left is telling you they want fewer messages, and a follow-up argues with that.

Time it inside 24 hours

Instagram only lets you message someone freely for 24 hours after their last interaction with you. A follow-up scheduled for the third day may simply not deliver. Put a delay of a few hours in front of it — long enough to be a genuine second attempt, short enough to land.

Writing one

Section titled “Writing one”
  • Don’t resend the first message. They either didn’t see it or weren’t convinced, and a copy fixes neither.
  • Keep it shorter than the first. One line and the link.
  • Give an out. “If it’s not for you, no worries at all” costs you nothing and stops the nudge reading as pressure.
  • One follow-up. Two is persistence, three is the block button.

A follow-up on Not seen message:

Hey — think this landed in your requests 👀 Here’s that link again in case it got buried.

title: Automation Settings: Run the Public Reply Without the DM
html:
Automation Settings: Run the Public Reply Without the DM

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The ⋯ button at the top right of the Setup direct message section holds the settings for the DM half of the automation.

Disable direct message

Section titled “Disable direct message”

One toggle, with a consequence worth reading twice: when disabled, only the public comment reply works.

Switch it on and the automation still watches the post, still matches your trigger, and still replies publicly under the comment. It just doesn’t send anything to anyone’s inbox. Everything you built in the DM section — the opener, the collect steps, the message, the follow-up — stays saved exactly as it is, and comes back the moment you switch it off.

When to use it

Section titled “When to use it”

Comment engagement without the DM load. Some posts want a lively comment section and nothing more. A public reply to every comment is engagement Instagram can see; a DM to every commenter is send volume you may not want to spend.

Testing your triggers safely. Publish with DMs disabled, comment from a second account, and confirm the right keywords fire and the public replies read well — without a single real person receiving a half-finished DM.

Pausing a campaign mid-flight. The offer sold out, the link broke, the code expired. Disabling the DM stops delivery immediately while the automation stays live and your comment section keeps answering. It’s a far lighter action than unpublishing, and nothing has to be rebuilt to resume.

A post that outgrew its automation. Something went unexpectedly viral and the DM volume is more than you want. Turn off the DM, keep the replies.

The public reply is now the whole message

With DMs off, the reply under the comment is all anyone gets — so “check your DMs!” becomes a promise the automation no longer keeps. Rewrite your public replies to stand on their own before you disable the DM, or people will go looking for a message that isn’t coming.

What it doesn’t do

Section titled “What it doesn’t do”

It doesn’t unpublish the automation, doesn’t clear the queue of DMs already scheduled behind a delay, and doesn’t affect any other automation on the account. It’s scoped to the DM section of the automation you’re editing.
