title: Post Automation Templates
html:
Post Automation Templates

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Building a post automation from scratch means deciding the trigger, the reply, the DM layout and the follow-up before you’ve seen one working. The template gallery skips that: nine ready-made post automations, each already wired for one common job, waiting for your post and your copy.

Opening the gallery

Section titled “Opening the gallery”

Click + New automation, then Browse templates at the foot of the dialog — it’s labelled 16 ready-made automations. Switch to the Basic tab to see the ones that open in the simple automation editor rather than the Flow builder.

Every card is labelled at the bottom with the automation type it creates, and the search box filters all 16 at once. Thirteen templates sit under Basic: the nine post automations below, three chat automations that answer keywords sent straight to your inbox, and one story automation.

The nine post templates

Section titled “The nine post templates”
Template What it does Built on
Auto-DM from comments
Popular		 DMs anyone who comments on a post or reel Comment-to-DM
Grow followers from comments
Popular		 Asks the commenter to follow you before it sends the content Ask to follow
Auto-DM on all posts and reels One automation covering every post and reel on the account Post selection
Auto-DM on next post or reel Arms itself and waits for your next upload to publish Post selection
Collect email/phone from comments Asks for an email or phone number before it hands over the content Collect email and phone
Auto-DM when someone shares your Post or Reel Replies when someone sends your post to their own inbox Share triggers
Re-engage with follow-up message Sends a second message on conditions and time delays to people who went quiet Follow-ups
Auto-DM from comments with an opener message Sends a short greeting with a button first, then the real content on the tap Opener message
Auto DM product link carousel Sends up to ten clickable links in a single swipeable message Carousels

Which one to start with

Section titled “Which one to start with”

Auto-DM from comments is the baseline. Everything else on the list is that automation with one thing added, so it’s the one to open if you want to understand the editor rather than just ship something.

Pick a more specific template when the shape of the campaign is already decided:

  • Running the same offer across your whole feed → Auto-DM on all posts and reels
  • Launching something tomorrow → Auto-DM on next post or reel, set up before you upload
  • Building a mailing list, not just clicks → Collect email/phone from comments
  • Growing the account rather than the list → Grow followers from comments
  • Sending several links at once → Auto DM product link carousel

The opener template is worth a look

Auto-DM from comments with an opener message exists because a cold DM with a link in it often lands in message requests. Sending a greeting with a button first gets the recipient to interact, which moves the conversation into the main inbox before your link arrives.

Making a template yours

Section titled “Making a template yours”

A template opens as an unpublished draft with a placeholder name and a Draft badge, so nothing goes out while you edit. Work down the editor:

1. Point it at a post. The Post card is the one thing no template can guess. Templates that say all posts or next post have already made this choice for you — check it’s the one you wanted.

2. Set the trigger words. Templates ship with generic keywords. Replace them with the word you’ll actually tell people to comment, or switch the trigger type to any word or intent match.

3. Rewrite the message. Placeholder copy reads like placeholder copy. Replace it, put your real link in, and use {{username}} where a name belongs. Then add variations so a hundred people don’t all receive the identical message.

4. Check the steps the template added. An opener, a collect-info step or a follow-up arrives pre-wired with its own copy and conditions — read those too, not just the main message.

5. Publish, then test from a second account. Comment your own keyword and watch the DM arrive. It’s the only check that covers the whole chain.

Templates are also worth reading

Opening a template close to what you want and looking at how it’s assembled is the fastest way to learn the editor — which steps were added, in what order, and what each one is for. You can close it without publishing.

title: Create an Instagram Story Automation
html:
Create an Instagram Story Automation

5 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

A story automation replies to the people who react to your story, answer it with a word, or tag you in a story of their own. Unlike a comment, all three of those arrive in your DMs already — so the automation isn’t opening a conversation, it’s answering one, which is why story replies convert well and why they’re easy to miss when there are two hundred of them.

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to LinktoDM
  • A story currently live on the account, if you want to point the automation at one specific story

Start a story automation

Section titled “Start a story automation”

Click + New automation and pick Story automation — replies to story replies and reactions — from the Quick automations row.

The editor opens as an unpublished draft in two halves: Setup triggers and public reply at the top, Setup direct message below. Stories have no comment section, so there’s no public reply step here — the whole automation is the DM.

1. Choose which story it watches

Section titled “1. Choose which story it watches”

The dropdown on the Story card decides what wakes the automation up. There are four choices, and they behave quite differently.

Option When it fires
apply for story mention Someone tags your account in their story
apply for all stories Anyone replies to or reacts to any story you post, now and in future
apply for next story The next story you upload, and only that one
a specific story One story you’re running right now, picked from the grid

apply for all stories is the set-and-forget option — post as usual and the automation keeps answering. a specific story suits a single campaign: a poll, a launch, a link you only want handled today.

Stories expire, so “a specific story” does too

The picker reads the stories currently live on your account. With none running it shows No story · Add a story and try again — and since Instagram stories last 24 hours, an automation tied to one specific story stops having anything to watch once that story is gone. Use all stories or next story for anything meant to keep running.

Story mentions are their own case. Choose apply for story mention and the Trigger card disappears entirely — the mention is the trigger, so there’s no keyword to match and nothing to set. The editor drops straight from Story to the message.

2. Set the trigger

Section titled “2. Set the trigger”

For the three reply-based options, the Trigger card decides which replies qualify.

  • any word — every reply and reaction qualifies. The right pick when the story says “reply anything for the link”, and the only one that catches emoji-only reactions reliably.
  • a specific word (s) — add keywords as chips, one per line, pressing Enter after each. Any one of them matching is enough.
  • intent match — describe what a reply should mean and let LinktoDM judge it, instead of guessing every spelling of “price”.

One DM per user sits below the keywords. With it on, someone who replies to your story five times still gets a single DM. Stories invite rapid-fire replies far more than comments do, so this is worth switching on more often here than on a post automation.

3. Write the DM

Section titled “3. Write the DM”

The Message card is the reply itself — plain text by default, with the dropdown offering the same layouts as a post automation: buttons, image cards, carousels and attachments.

You have 900 characters. Use {{username}} to drop in the replier’s name — it renders live in the preview on the right. Add variations generates up to five wordings of the same message that rotate automatically, which matters more on stories than anywhere else: the people replying to your story are often the same regulars, week after week.

4. Add the optional steps

Section titled “4. Add the optional steps”

Four buttons under the message add the steps that turn a reply into something more than an answer:

  • Opener message — a greeting with a button before the real DM
  • Collect info — ask for an email or phone number and save it to Contacts

5 min read

A story automation replies to the people who react to your story, answer it with a word, or tag you in a story of their own. An Instagram account connected to LinktoDM
A story currently live on the account, if you want to point the automation at one specific story
Start a story automation
Section titled “Start a story automation”

Four ways to point a story automation

apply for all stories	Anyone replies to or reacts to any story you post, now and in future
apply for next story	The next story you upload, and only that one
a specific story	One story you’re running right now, picked from the grid

apply for all stories is the set-and-forget option — post as usual and the automation keeps answering. a specific story suits a single campaign: a poll, a launch, a link you only want handled today.

The picker reads the stories currently live on your account. With none running it shows No story · Add a story and try again — and since Instagram stories last 24 hours, an automation tied to one specific story stops having anything to watch once that story is gone. Keyword chips, the trigger type dropdown, and the One DM per user toggle
any word — every reply and reaction qualifies. The right pick when the story says “reply anything for the link”, and the only one that catches emoji-only reactions reliably.
a specific word (s) — add keywords as chips, one per line, pressing Enter after each. Any one of them matching is enough.

900 characters, with variations above the box and the optional steps beneath it

title: Story Automation Templates
html:
Story Automation Templates

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The template gallery carries one story automation: Respond to story mentions. Open it from + New automation → Browse templates, on the Basic tab — the card is labelled Story automation at the foot.

Respond to story mentions

Section titled “Respond to story mentions”

Send a thank you message, offer, or link whenever someone mentions you in their story.

Someone tagging your account in their story is the warmest signal Instagram gives you, and it’s the one most accounts answer late or not at all. This template answers every one of them instantly.

What it arrives with

Section titled “What it arrives with”
  • Story card set to apply for story mention, showing Story mention selected. That’s the whole trigger.
  • No Trigger card at all. A mention needs no keyword to match, so the editor drops straight from the Story card to the DM — one card fewer than a reply-based story automation.
  • A plain-text message with five variations already generated, opening on something like helloo.. {{username}} Thank you for mentioning us.. — 51 of the 900 characters used.
  • The four optional steps unused — Opener message, Collect info, Ask to follow and Follow up message are all there to add.

What to change before publishing

Section titled “What to change before publishing”

Rewrite the message. The placeholder is deliberately bland. A thank-you on its own is a dead end; the mention is worth more if the reply carries something — a discount code, the link to the thing they tagged you about, or a question that keeps the thread going.

Then re-open the variations. They were generated from the placeholder, so they’ll paraphrase text you’ve just deleted. Regenerate or rewrite all five once your copy is final — message variations only help if every version is one you’d have sent.

Keep {{username}}. On a mention it lands well: the person tagged you by name, and being answered by name reads as a person noticing rather than a system firing.

Consider what comes next. People who tag you unprompted are the most likely to follow, subscribe or buy, so this is a natural place for Collect info or a follow-up — neither of which the template adds for you.

Mentions only reach you if the account is public

A story mention from a private account, or from someone who has restricted who can tag them, may never generate the notification the automation listens for. Nothing is misconfigured when a particular mention doesn’t fire.

The story automations with no template

Section titled “The story automations with no template”

Only mentions ship as a template. The other three story triggers — all stories, next story and a specific story — take about the same time to build from an empty story automation, since the Story card and one keyword are most of the work:

  • A link on every story — apply for all stories, trigger on any word, DM the link. Set it up once and every “link?” reply is answered from then on.
  • A launch story — apply for next story with a specific keyword, built the night before you post.
  • A poll or a quiz — a specific story, intent match on the answer you’re looking for, different DMs for different stories.

title: How Chat Automation Works
html:
How Chat Automation Works

Updated Sep 9, 2026

LinktoDM has three quick automations, and they’re told apart by where the person is when they set one off:

Automation Fires when someone…
Post automation Comments on your post or reel
Story automation Replies to, reacts to, or mentions your story
Chat automation Sends a keyword straight to your inbox

A chat automation has no post and no story attached to it. It watches your inbox, and when an incoming message contains one of your keywords it answers and takes over the conversation from there.

What a chat conversation is made of

Section titled “What a chat conversation is made of”

The chat editor isn’t the automation editor with cards, and it isn’t the flow canvas. It’s a script, written top to bottom in the order the conversation happens:

  1. A trigger — the keyword or keywords that start the script.
  2. Steps — each step is one message you send, up to 590 characters.
  3. Choices (optional) — buttons under a message. Add them and each choice gets its own branch with its own next message.
  4. A collect field (optional) — after a step, ask for an Email, a Phone number or Any answer, and the reply is validated and saved.

You add steps with Add Step and it grows downward. The phone on the right plays the whole thing back as a DM thread while you type, which is the fastest way to notice a script that reads like a form.

When to use one

Section titled “When to use one”

Chat automation is the answer to “DM me the word BOOK” — the call to action that lives in your bio, your captions, your story stickers, and on the slide at the end of a reel. The person has to message you first, so:

  • Bio and link-in-bio CTAs — “DM us PRICING” is a chat automation, not a post automation, because there’s no comment involved.
  • A front desk for the inbox — greet everyone who says hello and route them to the right answer with choices.
  • Lead capture — walk someone through email, then phone, then name, saving each answer to Contacts as it arrives.
  • A menu of products — list what you sell as buttons and let people pick.

Reach for a post automation instead whenever the trigger is a comment, and the Flow builder when you need conditions, delays, tags or a payment step — a chat script runs straight through and can’t branch on who the person is, only on which button they tapped.

What it doesn’t have

Section titled “What it doesn’t have”

Coming from a post automation, four things are missing, and their absence is the point rather than a gap:

  • No public reply. There’s no comment to reply under.
  • No post or story to choose. The keyword is the whole trigger.
  • No opener message. An opener exists to get someone to interact before you send a link — in a chat automation they already have.
  • No separate Collect info step. Collecting is built into the script itself, attached to whichever step asks the question.

They message you first, so the window is already open

Instagram lets you reply for 24 hours after someone’s last message. A chat automation always starts from an inbound DM, so that clock is running from the moment they typed your keyword — and a script that waits for an answer that never comes will run out of time rather than hang around.

Ready to build one — Create a chat automation.

title: Create an Instagram Chat Automation
html:
Create an Instagram Chat Automation

3 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

A chat automation answers people who message your inbox directly — the “DM me BOOK” call to action. This walks the editor from an empty script to a published automation.

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to LinktoDM
  • A second Instagram account to test from, since you can't DM yourself

Open the chat editor

Section titled “Open the chat editor”

Click + New automation, then Chat automation — replies to keywords sent in DMs. The editor opens on a single empty step with the trigger field above it and the DM preview on the right.

Rename it from Untitled using the pencil in the breadcrumb before you go further — chat automations are named after their keyword often enough that start and Untitled pile up fast.

1. Set the trigger keywords

Section titled “1. Set the trigger keywords”

Type the keywords to trigger and start the conversation sits above the script. Type a word and use commas to separate several — pricing, price, cost is one automation covering three spellings.

Choose words people would plausibly type on purpose. A keyword like hi catches every passing greeting; BOOK catches the people who read your caption.

How loosely they match

Section titled “How loosely they match”

The gear beside the trigger field opens two matching settings, and together they decide how forgiving your keyword is.

  • Any word — off by default. Switch it on and the automation replies to every incoming DM regardless of what it says. That’s the right setting for a general “thanks for reaching out” front desk, and the wrong one for anything triggered by a specific campaign word.
  • Trigger keyword within a sentence as well — on by default. It’s what makes “hey, can you send me the pricing?” match the keyword pricing. Uncheck it and the message has to be the keyword and nothing else — which is stricter than most people type, so leave it on unless you’re getting false matches.

Any word overrides your keywords

With Any word on, the keyword field stops deciding anything — every DM enters the script. Run at most one such automation per account, or two automations will answer the same message.

2. Write the first message

Section titled “2. Write the first message”

The first step is what they get back. 590 characters, counted under the box, which is shorter than a post automation’s DM — chat scripts are meant to be a back-and-forth rather than one long block.

Write it as the opening of a conversation, not a broadcast. The preview on the right shows it as a chat bubble the moment you stop typing, and a message that looked fine in the editor often looks like a wall in the thread.

3. Add the rest of the script

Section titled “3. Add the rest of the script”

Add Step appends the next message. Each step is one bubble, sent in order.

Two things turn a script from a monologue into a conversation, and both have their own page:

  • Choices — buttons under a message, each with its own branch and its own follow-on messages.
  • Collect fields — pause the script, wait for an email, phone number or free-text answer, and save it to Contacts.

Keep the first version short. Three steps you’ve tested beat eight you haven’t.

4. Publish and test

Section titled “4. Publish and test”

Publish is top right. Then message the account from your second Instagram account with the exact keyword and watch the script run.

Test the wrong input too — send something that doesn’t match and confirm nothing fires, then send the keyword mid-sentence and confirm it does. Those two checks tell you the matching settings are what you meant.

You should now have

A published chat automation that answers a keyword sent to your inbox, with the matching behaviour set deliberately rather than by default, and a test conversation run from a second account.

Collect fields — pause the script, wait for an email, phone number or free-text answer, and save it to Contacts.

Keep the first version short. Three steps you’ve tested beat eight you haven’t.

4. Publish and test
Section titled “4. Publish and test”

Publish is top right. Then message the account from your second Instagram account with the exact keyword and watch the script run.

Test the wrong input too — send something that doesn’t match and confirm nothing fires, then send the keyword mid-sentence and confirm it does. Those two checks tell you the matching settings are what you meant.

You should now have

A published chat automation that answers a keyword sent to your inbox, with the matching behaviour set deliberately rather than by default, and a test conversation run from a second account.

title: Chat Choices, Branches and Collecting Replies
html:
Chat Choices, Branches and Collecting Replies

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A script that only sends messages is a broadcast with extra steps. Two features turn it into a conversation: choices, which let the person pick a direction, and collect fields, which let the script wait for something they type.

Adding choices

Section titled “Adding choices”

Under every message is an Add choice field — type a label, press Enter, and it becomes a chip. Each chip renders as a tappable button beneath that message in the DM.

Add a choice and a new row appears: Select a choice and enter a message for each option, with one tab per choice. Selecting a tab shows that branch’s script, and the box below is prompted with the choice’s name — Type message for “DS”.

Every branch needs a message. An empty one shows Required field in red and the automation won’t publish until it’s filled. That’s deliberate: a button that leads nowhere is worse than no button.

A few things worth knowing before you build a deep tree:

  • Choices are the only branching a chat script has. It can’t branch on who the person is, whether they follow you, or what they said in free text — that’s what the Conditions node in the Flow builder is for.
  • Branches carry on independently. Each one can have its own steps, its own further choices, and its own collect fields.
  • Keep the labels short. They’re buttons in a chat bubble, so two or three words read best — Get expert tips, Discover products.

Collecting a reply

Section titled “Collecting a reply”

A collect field pauses the script, waits for the person to type, validates what they send, and saves it to their contact record.

The field sits between two steps: the message above asks the question, the field catches the answer, and the step below responds to it. Ask plainly — the field validates the format, but it can’t make an unexplained prompt feel less abrupt.

Email, Phone or Any

Section titled “Email, Phone or Any”

The dropdown on the collect field decides what counts as a valid answer.

Type Accepts
Email A valid email address
Phone A phone number
Any Whatever they type — names, a city, an open answer

Email and Phone land in Contacts alongside everything collected by your post automations, ready to export or push into your CRM with Zapier.

Any is the one to be careful with — it accepts anything, including “why?”, so only use it where a wrong answer costs nothing.

The trash icon beside the dropdown removes the field, leaving the messages either side of it intact.

Ask for one thing at a time

Every collect field is a point where someone can stop replying, and the drop-off compounds. Ask for the email while they still want the thing you promised, and leave the phone number and the name for automations where you genuinely need them.

A worked shape

Section titled “A worked shape”

The pattern most chat scripts end up in:

  1. Greet and offer choices — “What are you here for?” with two or three buttons.
  2. Branch — each button gets a message that actually answers it.
  3. Collect where it’s earned — ask for the email in the branch where you’re about to send something by email, not at the top for everyone.
  4. Confirm — a short closing message so the thread doesn’t end on their reply.

The Capture leads and Sell templates are both this shape, already built.

title: Chat Automation Templates
html:
Chat Automation Templates

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Three of the thirteen templates on the Basic tab of the template gallery are chat automations. Between them they cover the three jobs an inbox script usually does: answer everyone, collect details, and sell something.

Open them from + New automation → Browse templates, on the Basic tab — each card is labelled Chat automation at the foot.

Respond to all your DMs

Section titled “Respond to all your DMs”

Reply automatically when someone sends you a direct message with specific keywords. — Popular

What it arrives with — the keyword Hello and a single step: Thanks for reaching out!. How can we assist you today? at 54 of 590 characters. No choices, no collect field.

What to change. Two decisions, both above the message:

  • The keyword. Hello only catches people who open with a greeting. Either swap it for the word your bio actually tells people to send, or open the gear settings and switch Any word on so it answers every incoming DM — which is what “respond to all your DMs” implies, and isn’t how the template ships.
  • The dead end. The message asks a question the script has no way to answer. Add choices so the reply routes somewhere, or accept that this one is an acknowledgement that buys you time to reply yourself.

Capture leads from DMs

Section titled “Capture leads from DMs”

Reply to incoming DM’s leads and guide them to submit their email or phone number.

What it arrives with — the keyword connect and an alternating script: a message, then a collect field, three times over.

  1. Just drop email, and I’ll send all the good stuff straight to your inbox! → Email field
  2. What’s your contact number? → Phone field
  3. What’s your name? → a free-text field, then a closing Thank you for providing contact details, We will connect soon.

Everything it captures lands in Contacts.

What to change. Mainly: cut a question. Three prompts in a row is an interrogation, and every one of them is somewhere the person can stop replying. Unless you genuinely call leads, delete the phone step with the trash icon beside its field and keep the email.

Then rewrite the first message so it says what they get. “Drop your email and I’ll send the pricing guide” converts; “all the good stuff” doesn’t.

Sell products or services from DMs

Section titled “Sell products or services from DMs”

List products or services and guide users to purchase them directly from your DMs.

What it arrives with — the keyword Hello, the greeting Hey! We’re so excited to have you here! How can I help you?, and two choices: Get expert tips and Discover products.

What to change. The branches are empty — Type message for “Get expert tips” is a placeholder, and an empty branch is a Required field that blocks publishing. So this template is a shape rather than a finished automation, and the work is writing the two paths behind the buttons.

Rename the choices to your actual categories while you’re there. Discover products is a placeholder; See the pricing and Book a call are decisions someone can make.

Start from Capture leads even if you’re selling

Capture leads is the only one of the three that arrives complete enough to publish and watch working. Open it first to see how a collect field behaves in a live thread, then build the selling script knowing what the pieces do.

Building one from scratch

Section titled “Building one from scratch”

None of the three is much work to reproduce — Create a chat automation walks the editor end to end, and choices and collect fields covers the two parts that do the real work.

title: Flow Builder Wiring Basics: Nodes, Handles and Connectors
html:
Flow Builder Wiring Basics: Nodes, Handles and Connectors

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A flow is a set of nodes on a canvas, joined by lines. One node sends a message, another waits, another checks a condition, and the lines decide what runs after what.

Open it from + New automation → Flow builder (“drag and connect the steps yourself”). Every new flow starts as a Draft with one empty Begin when… block, waiting for a trigger.

Adding a node

Section titled “Adding a node”

Click + on the canvas → pick a node type → configure it in the panel that opens on the right → connect it to the next step.

The node types

Section titled “The node types”
Node What it does
Trigger Starts the flow when something happens on Instagram
Send message Sends an Instagram DM
Action Updates contact data or talks to outside tools
Conditions Checks something and branches the flow
Delay Pauses before continuing
Randomizer Splits contacts across several paths at random
Payment Creates a payment link and branches on whether it’s paid

Nodes run in order, following the lines — unless a Conditions node splits the path in two.

Connecting nodes

Section titled “Connecting nodes”

Every node has a small circle on its right edge. That’s a handle, and it’s what you drag to build the flow.

Two ways to do it:

  • Click + on the canvas and pick a node, or
  • Drag the Then handle off your current node and drop it where you want the next step

Then vs. Next step

Section titled “Then vs. Next step”

Most nodes have one Then handle: do this, then go there.

Four cases give you more:

  • A Send message node with a Collect user info block waits for the contact’s reply, so it gets a Next step handle for what happens once the answer arrives, alongside Then.
  • A Conditions node replaces Then with two handles — Yes and Doesn’t match any — one for each path.
  • A Randomizer node replaces Then with one handle per variation — A, B, C… — one for each path a contact can be sent down.
  • A Payment node keeps Then and adds Payment successful and Payment failed below it, so the outcome of the charge routes the flow.

Leave a handle unwired and the flow simply stops for anyone who reaches it.

Duplicating and deleting

Section titled “Duplicating and deleting”

Hover a node and a small toolbar appears above it: duplicate it (handy for a message you want to send twice with different wording) or delete it. Deleting a node also removes the lines into and out of it, so re-wire its neighbours afterwards.

Pro Tip

The controls at the bottom-left zoom in, zoom out, fit the whole flow on screen, and lock the canvas. Lock it once a flow is wired the way you want — it stops you dragging a node loose while you’re panning around.

title: Trigger Node: Start a Flow in the Flow Builder
html:
Trigger Node: Start a Flow in the Flow Builder

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Every flow has to start somewhere, and that’s what a Trigger is. It’s the event that wakes your automation up and gets it moving.

No trigger, no flow. It’s step one, always.

Setting one up

Section titled “Setting one up”
  1. Click + New Trigger in the Begin when… block
  2. Pick the event that should kick things off
  3. Set any conditions the trigger needs
  4. Connect it to your first step

Available triggers

Section titled “Available triggers”
Trigger Fires when…
User comments on your Post or Reel Someone comments on a post or reel
User replies to your Story Someone replies to your story
User sends a message Someone DMs you
User mentions you in a Story You get story-mentioned
User shares a post or reel Someone shares your content via DM

Narrowing a trigger

Section titled “Narrowing a trigger”

A trigger doesn’t have to fire on everything. Once you’ve picked the event, set the condition that goes with it — a User sends a message trigger can listen for any message, or only ones containing a keyword like hello, exactly like the keyword triggers in a basic automation.

The node shows what it settled on: the event on top, the condition underneath.

Pro Tip

Start with the event you can test yourself. Comment on your own post from a second account, or DM yourself the keyword, and watch the flow run before you point it at anything that matters.

Where to go next

Section titled “Where to go next”

With the trigger in place, drag its Then handle to the first real step — usually a Send message node.

title: Send Message Node: Layouts and Content Blocks
html:
Send Message Node: Layouts and Content Blocks

Updated Sep 9, 2026

This is how your flow actually talks to people. Add the node, pick a layout, and write the message in the panel on the right.

Content blocks

Section titled “Content blocks”

One node can send more than one thing. + Add more content blocks stacks another block underneath the first, and they go out in the order you stacked them.

Block Sends Use this for
Text A simple text message Welcomes, quick replies, instructions
Text with buttons A message + action buttons Menus, FAQs, guided conversations
Card with image One image + title + subtitle + buttons Product highlights, promos, announcements
Carousel Multiple scrollable image cards Catalogs, multiple offers, step-by-step content
Attachment An image, video, voice note or PDF Lead magnets, guides, demos
Collect user info A prompt for email, phone or any custom field Lead gen, registration, onboarding

Personalising the message

Section titled “Personalising the message”

Type {{username}} to drop in the recipient’s Instagram username. It shows up in the editor as a blue Username chip, and each contact sees their own handle. A text block holds up to 850 characters, counted for you under the box.

Setup

Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → pick your layout → fill in the content → connect to the next step.

Waiting for an answer

Section titled “Waiting for an answer”

Collect user info is the one block that pauses the conversation: the node shows Waiting for Email from contact and holds until they reply. That’s why it gets its own Next step handle — Then carries on immediately, Next step runs once the answer is in.

Pro Tip

html:
Action Node: Tags, Custom Fields and API Requests

Updated Sep 9, 2026

While other nodes control where the flow goes, the Action node changes what LinktoDM knows — updating contact info, managing tags, or reaching out to other tools.

Setup

Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → click + Add an action → pick the action → configure it → connect to the next step.

Available actions

Section titled “Available actions”
Action Does Use this for
Add contact tag Adds one or more tags to the contact Segmenting by interest, campaign, or behavior
Remove contact tag Removes one or more tags Clearing “Lead” once they convert
Set user field Saves a value to a custom field on the contact Storing language, membership level, source campaign
Make external API request Sends data to a webhook or external service Pushing leads to a CRM, triggering your own backend
Delete contact Permanently removes the contact from your audience ⚠️ Irreversible — use carefully

One node can hold several actions: + Add action stacks another underneath, and they run together before the flow moves on.

Setting a user field

Section titled “Setting a user field”

Set user field asks for three things: which user field to write to, the operation (set a value, and the other operations the field type allows), and the value itself. Don’t have a suitable field yet? + Create new field makes one without leaving the panel.

Two things worth knowing about the value:

  • {{system.last_input}} saves whatever the contact most recently replied, which is how a Collect user info answer gets stored on the contact.
  • The value is converted to the field’s type, so a number field takes a number and a true/false field takes True or False.

Tags vs. custom fields, quickly

Section titled “Tags vs. custom fields, quickly”

Tags are labels, and a contact can have several. Custom fields hold actual values — an email, a tier, a language. Use tags to segment, use fields to store.

Example flow

Section titled “Example flow”

Delete contact can’t be undone

Deleting a contact removes their record permanently, including anything you’d collected from them. Put it behind a condition you trust, and test the flow on your own second account before publishing.

title: Conditions Node: Branch a Flow with Yes and No Paths
html:
Conditions Node: Branch a Flow with Yes and No Paths

Updated Sep 9, 2026

This is where flows get smart. A Conditions node checks something about the user or contact, then sends them down one of two paths:

  • Yes — the condition matched
  • Doesn’t match any — it didn’t

Each is its own handle on the right edge of the node, so the flow physically forks on the canvas.

Setup

Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → pick a condition type → set the value → wire up both the Yes and Doesn’t-match paths.

Available condition types

Section titled “Available condition types”
Condition Checks Use this for
If User Followed Me Whether they follow you Gating exclusive content to followers
If Business Follows User Whether you follow them back VIP-style flows for accounts you already follow
Verified on Instagram Whether their account is verified Routing verified users to a dedicated path
Followers Count Their follower count, with > / < / = Offering partnerships to accounts over a threshold
Contact Email Whether you already have their email saved Skipping the ask if you already have it
Contact Phone Whether you already have their phone saved Same idea, for phone number
Custom Field Any custom value you’ve stored on the contact Branching by language, membership tier, etc.

Collect the data first

Email, phone and custom fields only work once they’ve been collected — usually via a Collect user info block earlier in the flow, or a Set user field action. With nothing stored, the check has nothing to match and everyone takes the Doesn’t-match path.

Example

Section titled “Example”

Both paths need somewhere to go. An unwired branch is a dead end — the flow simply stops for anyone who lands on it.

Pro Tip

Conditions pair naturally with the Action node: branch on whether someone follows you, then set a field or add a tag on each path, and you’ve classified every contact who comes through the flow.

title: Delay Node: Pause a Flow Before the Next Step
html:
Delay Node: Pause a Flow Before the Next Step

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Sometimes the best move is to wait a beat. The Delay node pauses the flow for a set amount of time before moving on — handy for spacing out messages so the conversation feels human instead of like a wall of texts.

Setup

Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → enter a duration → pick seconds, minutes, hours or days → connect to the next step.

The node reads back what you set — Wait 1 minutes and continue — so you can check a flow’s timing without opening every node.

Use this for

Section titled “Use this for”
  • Waiting before a follow-up message
  • Breaking up multi-step convos so they don’t feel like spam
  • Delaying a promo or reminder to a better moment

Nothing downstream runs until the delay finishes — then the flow picks up right where it left off.

Pro Tip

A few seconds between two messages is usually enough to stop them landing as one block. Save hours and days for follow-ups, where the point is to come back later rather than to look human.

title: Randomizer Node: Split a Flow Across Random Paths
html:
Randomizer Node: Split a Flow Across Random Paths

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The Randomizer node forks a flow into several paths and sends each contact down one of them by chance, in the proportions you set. Two people who send you the same word can get two different replies.

Which path someone lands on says nothing about them — it isn’t based on anything you know about the contact, only on the odds you set. That’s what makes it a fair way to compare two versions of a message.

Setup

Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → set each variation’s share → wire every variation to its own next step → decide whether the choice sticks to the contact.

A new Randomizer starts with four variations — A, B, C and D at 25% each. Each has a colour, a slider, a percentage box, and its own handle on the right edge of the node, so the flow physically forks four ways on the canvas.

Splitting the traffic

Section titled “Splitting the traffic”

Drag a slider or type into the percentage box. + New Variation adds another path; you don’t have to keep all four, and two is the usual shape for an A/B test.

Percentages are odds, not quotas

A 50/50 split doesn’t deal contacts out alternately. Each contact is an independent roll, so across 20 people you might see 13 and 7. The split gets closer to what you set as the numbers grow — which is why an A/B test needs to run for a while before its result means anything.

Sticky, or re-rolled every time

Section titled “Sticky, or re-rolled every time”

One toggle changes what the node fundamentally does: Pick a random path every time.

Toggle What a returning contact gets
Off (default) The variation they were given the first time, on every later trigger
On A fresh roll each time they trigger the flow — they can land somewhere different

Which one you want follows from why you’re splitting:

  • Leave it off for A/B tests. You’re comparing two versions, and someone who sees both is in neither group. Off also means a contact’s experience stays consistent — they don’t get a different greeting every time they message you.
  • Turn it on when the roll is the feature. Rotating offers, a lucky draw, or spreading enquiries across your team all want a fresh result each time.

When the total isn’t 100%

Section titled “When the total isn’t 100%”

The shares have to add up. Go over or under and the Assigned traffic figure turns red, the node on the canvas says so — Distribution totals 103% — must equal 100% — and a Split evenly link appears in the panel to reset every variation to an equal share.

Example: which payment gateway converts better?

Section titled “Example: which payment gateway converts better?”

Split contacts evenly between two Payment nodes — one charging through Stripe, one through Razorpay — and let them run. The Payment successful counts tell you which checkout your audience actually completes.

Leave the toggle off for this one. A contact who paid through Stripe last week should not be quoted Razorpay today.

Use this for

Section titled “Use this for”
  • A/B testing an opener — two variations, same next step, different wording
  • Rotating offers — an uneven split, so a small share gets the better code
  • Rolling out a change carefully — 90% down the flow you trust, 10% down the rewrite
  • Spreading enquiries across a team — four variations, four handoff messages

Wire every variation

An unwired variation is a dead end, and a silent one: with a four-way split, leaving D unconnected means a quarter of everyone who triggers the flow gets nothing at all and no error anywhere says so. Check each handle has a line leaving it before you publish.

Pro Tip

Make the variations tell themselves apart. Two messages that both open with “Hey!” are impossible to distinguish in Flow analytics a week later, when the per-node Sent and Clicked counts are the whole reason you split the traffic in the first place.

title: Payment Node: Collect a Payment Inside a Flow
html:
Payment Node: Collect a Payment Inside a Flow

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The Payment node — Collect payment on the canvas — takes money inside the conversation, so a flow can go from interest to paid without sending the contact off to a checkout page you built somewhere else.

The node creates the link. It doesn’t send it.

This is the one thing to get right. Collect payment asks your gateway for a payment link and saves it to a user field. Nothing reaches the contact until a Send message node after it puts that field into a message. Wire the node, skip the message, and the flow charges no one — the link is created and then sits there unread.

Setup

Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → connect a payment gateway → set the amount and what it’s for → send the link → wire up the success and failure paths.

The panel is a short wizard. The first time, it’s four steps — you’re connecting a gateway before you can charge anything. Once an account is connected it drops to two, because the connect steps are behind you.

Step 1 — Connect a payment gateway

Section titled “Step 1 — Connect a payment gateway”

A new node shows Connect payment gateway instead of an amount. Click it and pick your provider:

Provider Takes Notes
Stripe Cards, wallets · 135+ currencies Best for international customers
Razorpay UPI, cards, netbanking Best for customers paying in India

Step 2 — Enter your API keys

Section titled “Step 2 — Enter your API keys”

Whichever provider you picked, LinktoDM needs keys from that account to create links on your behalf.

Stripe — from your Stripe dashboard, under Developers → API keys. One field: the secret key.

Razorpay — from your Razorpay dashboard, under Settings → API keys. Two fields: Key ID and Key secret.

Use a standard Stripe key, not a restricted one

A restricted key (rk_) can be missing the permissions needed to create payment links and receive payment updates, and the failure shows up later as links that never generate. Use the Standard secret key (sk_) with full access.

Keys are encrypted at rest. The secret is hidden once saved and can only be replaced, never read back — so if you need it again, get a fresh one from your provider’s dashboard.

Click Connect and the account is saved to your workspace. Every later Payment node picks it from a list instead of asking for keys again.

A Test badge on a row means that account is on test keys. Real cards won’t be charged, which is what you want while you’re building the flow — and what you must remember to swap before publishing it.

Step 3 — Set the amount

Section titled “Step 3 — Set the amount”
Field What it does
Amount The charge, plus the currency it’s in. The panel reads back the currency and its decimal places — Indian Rupee · 2 decimal places
What they’re paying for The line item the customer sees at checkout, and the label on the node afterwards
Description Optional detail under it
Save payment link The user field the generated link is written to. + Create new field makes one without leaving the panel

The panel tells you the variable it just created: later nodes can send the link as {{user.payment_link}}.

Save, and the node on the canvas shows the charge it will create — Razorpay · ₹10.00 · webservices — so you can read a flow’s pricing without opening it.

Step 4 — Send the link

Section titled “Step 4 — Send the link”

The node now has three handles down its right edge:

Handle Fires when
Then The link has been created — immediately, before anyone pays
Payment successful The customer completes the payment
Payment failed The payment doesn’t go through

Then is the one that matters here. Wire it to a Send message node, and in the message body type {{ — the user field picker opens with the payment fields in it.

Pick Payment link and it drops in as a chip. That message is what the contact actually receives — the tappable link that opens checkout.

Three fields come out of the node, all available the same way:

  • payment_link — the checkout link
  • date_of_payment — the date it was paid
  • date_time_of_payment — the date and time

Example flow

Section titled “Example flow”

text:
Payment Node: Collect a Payment Inside a Flow

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The Payment node — Collect payment on the canvas — takes money inside the conversation, so a flow can go from interest to paid without sending the contact off to a checkout page you built somewhere else.

The node creates the link. It doesn’t send it.

This is the one thing to get right. Collect payment asks your gateway for a payment link and saves it to a user field. Nothing reaches the contact until a Send message node after it puts that field into a message. Wire the node, skip the message, and the flow charges no one — the link is created and then sits there unread.

Setup
Section titled “Setup”

Add the node → connect a payment gateway → set the amount and what it’s for → send the link → wire up the success and failure paths.

The panel is a short wizard. The first time, it’s four steps — you’re connecting a gateway before you can charge anything. Once an account is connected it drops to two, because the connect steps are behind you.

Step 1 — Connect a payment gateway
Section titled “Step 1 — Connect a payment gateway”

A new node shows Connect payment gateway instead of an amount. Click it and pick your provider:

PROVIDER	TAKES	NOTES
Stripe	Cards, wallets · 135+ currencies	Best for international customers
Razorpay	UPI, cards, netbanking	Best for customers paying in India
Step 1: pick the provider. Nothing is charged until a customer completes a payment.
Step 2 — Enter your API keys
Section titled “Step 2 — Enter your API keys”

Whichever provider you picked, LinktoDM needs keys from that account to create links on your behalf.

Stripe — from your Stripe dashboard, under Developers → API keys. One field: the secret key.

Stripe wants a Standard secret key — one that starts with sk_

Razorpay — from your Razorpay dashboard, under Settings → API keys. Two fields: Key ID and Key secret.

Razorpay needs both halves: the Key ID and its secret

Use a standard Stripe key, not a restricted one

A restricted key (rk_) can be missing the permissions needed to create payment links and receive payment updates, and the failure shows up later as links that never generate. Use the Standard secret key (sk_) with full access.

Keys are encrypted at rest. The secret is hidden once saved and can only be replaced, never read back — so if you need it again, get a fresh one from your provider’s dashboard.

Click Connect and the account is saved to your workspace. Every later Payment node picks it from a list instead of asking for keys again.

Connected accounts, with the account ID under each name — a Test badge means test keys

A Test badge on a row means that account is on test keys. Real cards won’t be charged, which is what you want while you’re building the flow — and what you must remember to swap before publishing it.

Step 3 — Set the amount
Section titled “Step 3 — Set the amount”
Payment details: what to charge, what it's for, and which field holds the link
FIELD	WHAT IT DOES
Amount	The charge, plus the currency it’s in. The panel reads back the currency and its decimal places — Indian Rupee · 2 decimal places
What they’re paying for	The line item the customer sees at checkout, and the label on the node afterwards
Description	Optional detail under it
Save payment link	The user field the generated link is written to. + Create new field makes one without leaving the panel

The panel tells you the variable it just created: later nodes can send the link as {{user.payment_link}}.

Save, and the node on the canvas shows the charge it will create — Razorpay · ₹10.00 · webservices — so you can read a flow’s pricing without opening it.

Step 4 — Send the link
Section titled “Step 4 — Send the link”

The node now has three handles down its right edge:

HANDLE	FIRES WHEN
Then	The link has been created — immediately, before anyone pays
Payment successful	The customer completes the payment
Payment failed	The payment doesn’t go through

Then is the one that matters here. Wire it to a Send message node, and in the message body type {{ — the user field picker opens with the payment fields in it.

Typing {{ in a message offers the fields the Payment node fills in

Pick Payment link and it drops in as a chip. That message is what the contact actually receives — the tappable link that opens checkout.

The finished shape: link on Then, confirmation on Payment successful, recovery on Payment failed

Three fields come out of the node, all available the same way:

payment_link — the checkout link
date_of_payment — the date it was paid
date_time_of_payment — the date and time
Example flow
Section titled “Example flow”
Trigger: message contains "pay"
  ↓
Send message: "Here's the link 👇"
  ↓
Collect payment: ₹10.00 · webservices
  ├── Then              → Send message: {{payment_link}}
  ├── Payment successful → Send message: "Payment received — here's your access"
  └── Payment failed     → Send message: "That didn't go through. Try again?"

Leave Payment successful or Payment failed unwired and the flow just stops for whoever lands there — a paying customer hearing nothing back is the worst version of a dead end.

Pro Tip

Test the whole path on a second account with test keys before you publish, and follow it all the way to the confirmation message. The node reporting success only means the gateway said so — it doesn’t tell you the contact ever got a link they could tap.

title: AI Flow Builder: Build a Flow from a Prompt
html:
AI Flow Builder: Build a Flow from a Prompt

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Don’t want to click through every node by hand? Describe the automation in plain English and let the Flow Assistant build it for you.

Start it from + New automation → AI assisted flow builder, or from the Describe the flow you want to build… bar at the bottom of the Flow builder canvas.

Premium

The Flow Assistant is part of the Premium plan.

How it works

Section titled “How it works”

Describe what you want → answer anything the assistant asks → watch it build → review the generated flow → edit as needed → publish.

It asks before it guesses

Section titled “It asks before it guesses”

The assistant doesn’t invent the parts of your request you left out. Ask it to classify contacts by whether they follow you and it will come back with the one thing it can’t infer — which trigger should start the flow — and let you tick the events you want.

Then it builds, narrating each node as it goes — nodes added, and the connections wired between them.

Example prompts

Section titled “Example prompts”
  • “When someone comments ‘link’ on my post, send them the download link.”
  • “If a follower sends pricing, tag them as a lead and send our pricing brochure.”
  • “Collect email addresses from users who comment FREEBIE.”
  • “Classify my clients by setting the client field true or false based on whether they’ve followed me.”

Use this for

Section titled “Use this for”

Getting a working starting point fast, especially if node-by-node building feels intimidating at first. What it produces is an ordinary flow — every node is one you could have added yourself, and every one of them is editable.

Always review before publishing

Section titled “Always review before publishing”

Check that the trigger, message content, conditions and actions match what you actually meant. Treat it as a first draft from a very fast intern, not a finished flow.

Pro Tip

Clear conversation starts the assistant fresh. Worth doing before an unrelated request, so it isn’t still working from the flow you described three prompts ago.

title: Flow Analytics: See How Your Automations Perform
html:
Flow Analytics: See How Your Automations Perform

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A published flow is a guess until you look at the numbers. LinktoDM reports on your automations in two places.

The Automations list

Section titled “The Automations list”

Every automation you’ve built is listed here with its own figures alongside it, including Clicks, and the toggle that shows whether it’s currently running. It’s the quickest read: which automations are live, and which are actually being used.

Stats

Section titled “Stats”

Stats in the left sidebar is the fuller view, across your account rather than one automation at a time.

Numbers only count while a flow is live

A flow in Draft hasn’t sent anything, and a paused one has stopped. If an automation shows nothing at all, check its toggle in the Automations list before you go looking for a problem in the flow itself.

Reading the result

Section titled “Reading the result”

The numbers are most useful as a comparison, not an absolute:

  • Barely any triggers — the trigger is too narrow. A specific keyword that nobody thinks to type catches nothing; try any-word and see how the volume changes.
  • Triggers but no clicks — the DM is the problem, not the automation. Try a different layout, a shorter message, or a clearer call to action.
  • A branch nobody reaches — a Conditions node is matching everyone one way. Check that whatever it tests has actually been collected earlier in the flow.

Change one thing at a time between checks. Two edits at once and the numbers can’t tell you which one worked.

html:
Flow Templates: Start From a Ready-Made Automation

Updated Sep 9, 2026

An empty canvas is the slowest way to start. The template gallery holds 16 ready-made automations, and the Flow tab filters it down to the ones that open on the flow canvas rather than in the simple editor. Any of them can be opened, edited and published as your own.

Opening the template gallery

Section titled “Opening the template gallery”

Click + New automation, then Browse templates at the foot of the dialog, and switch to the Flow tab. The Basic tab beside it holds the post, story and chat templates that run in the simple editor.

Making a template yours

Section titled “Making a template yours”

A template is a starting point, not a finished automation. Once it opens in the Flow builder, go through it the same way you’d review your own work:

  • The trigger — point it at your post, reel or keyword. This is the part a template can’t guess.
  • The message content — replace the placeholder copy and links with yours, and check it sounds like you.
  • Any conditions and actions — tags and custom fields in a template refer to names that may not exist in your account yet.

Then publish, and test it from a second account before you point real traffic at it.

Pro Tip

Templates are also the fastest way to read a good flow. Open one close to what you want, see how it’s wired, and you’ll know how to build the next one from scratch.

title: DM Queue
html:
DM Queue

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Every automated DM LinktoDM sends passes through a queue before it goes out. This page covers what that queue is, why it’s there, and where to view it.

What is the DM queue?

Section titled “What is the DM queue?”

The DM queue is a buffer between your automations and Instagram. When an automation sends a DM, the message is added to the queue first. LinktoDM then processes queued messages at a controlled rate instead of sending everything at once.

The queue is per account: every connected Instagram account or Facebook Page has its own.

Why does LinktoDM use a queue?

Section titled “Why does LinktoDM use a queue?”

Automations produce messages at whatever rate your audience produces comments, and that rate is uneven. A post that performs well can trigger hundreds of DMs in minutes.

  • Automations can generate large bursts of messages.
  • Instagram and Facebook both limit how quickly an account can send messages.
  • Sending a large number of messages simultaneously can result in failed deliveries or restrictions on the account.

The queue absorbs the burst so that delivery stays within the limits Meta applies to your account. For the limits themselves, see rate limits and throttling.

How the queue works

Section titled “How the queue works”

When an automation triggers a DM, LinktoDM adds the message to the queue. Messages are then processed at a controlled rate and sent as capacity becomes available.

Follow-up messages and delays also use the queue, but wait on their scheduled time rather than on sending capacity. For the full path a message takes, see how the queue works.

View the DM queue

Section titled “View the DM queue”

You can view queued messages from In queue in the console sidebar, below your automations and above Settings. Click it to expand the panel.

The panel shows how many follow-ups and DMs are pending, the rate messages are currently going out at, and the controls to pause delivery or clear the queue. For how to read those numbers, see queue status.

What happens when messages are queued?

Section titled “What happens when messages are queued?”
  • Messages wait in the queue until they’re ready to send.
  • The queue may grow during high-volume activity, such as a post receiving a large number of comments.
  • Messages are processed automatically — no action is required to release them.
  • A queue of 0 means there are currently no pending messages, which is the normal state while an automation is running.

title: How the DM Queue Works
html:
How the DM Queue Works

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A message your automation sends doesn’t go out the instant its trigger matches. It goes into the DM queue first, and LinktoDM releases it from there at a rate Meta accepts. This page covers what happens to a message while it’s in the queue.

The trip a message makes

Section titled “The trip a message makes”

Every message takes the same four steps:

  1. A trigger matches — someone comments, replies to a story, or a follow-up comes due.
  2. LinktoDM builds the message and puts it in the queue.
  3. The queue releases messages at a steady rate rather than all at once.
  4. Each one goes out and leaves the count.

Under normal traffic the whole trip takes seconds, which is why the queue is usually invisible: the count sits at 0 because messages leave as fast as they arrive. It becomes visible only when messages arrive faster than the safe rate lets them leave — the moment a post spikes — and that is exactly when you want it there.

Two kinds of waiting

Section titled “Two kinds of waiting”

Not everything in the queue is waiting for the same reason, which is why the queue panel counts them separately.

  • DMs are waiting on sending speed. They’re ready now; the queue is spacing them out. This is the number that moves during a spike.
  • Follow-ups are waiting on time. A follow-up step or a delay told them to go out later, and they sit in the queue until their timer says otherwise. A follow-up scheduled for tomorrow is in the queue all day, and that’s the feature working.

What the queue guarantees

Section titled “What the queue guarantees”

Nothing is dropped while it waits. A queued message is a message that will be sent, just not this second. It survives the wait, and the only things that remove it are being sent or being cleared by you.

It’s per account. The panel sits under the account switcher because the queue does too: every connected Instagram account or Facebook Page has its own, so a busy account and a quiet one don’t share a backlog.

The one thing the queue doesn’t do is go faster on request. There’s no priority lane and no setting to raise the rate; when Meta tightens, LinktoDM slows down deliberately so that the messages still get through.

Common questions

Section titled “Common questions”

Does the queue delay every DM? Technically yes, in practice no. Every message passes through it, but under normal traffic it’s out again in seconds. The delay only becomes noticeable when a post generates messages faster than the safe rate can release them.

Why does my queue say 0 when an automation is live? Because it’s keeping up. A count of 0 is the normal state, not a sign that nothing is firing. To confirm an automation is running, use its Hits column in the Automations list.

Can I make it send faster? No, and that’s the point. The rate is set by what the platform will accept from your account at that moment, not by a plan or a setting. The lever you do have is upstream: send fewer messages by tightening the trigger or by running fewer automations on the same account at once.

Will a queued message expire if it waits too long? No. Waiting doesn’t discard a message. It leaves the queue by being sent or by being cleared by you, and nothing else.

A follow-up is scheduled for next week — does it sit in the queue that whole time? Yes, and that’s expected. Follow-ups wait on their timer rather than on sending speed, so a large Follow-ups count on an account running long delays is normal.

Do my accounts share one queue? No. Every connected account has its own queue and its own rate, so a launch on one account doesn’t slow the others down.

Does pausing the queue switch my automations off? No. Triggers keep matching and messages keep piling up behind the pause — they’re delayed, not cancelled. To stop sending for longer than a few minutes, switch the automation off instead.

text:
How the DM Queue Works

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A message your automation sends doesn’t go out the instant its trigger matches. It goes into the DM queue first, and LinktoDM releases it from there at a rate Meta accepts. This page covers what happens to a message while it’s in the queue.

The trip a message makes
Section titled “The trip a message makes”

Every message takes the same four steps:

A trigger matches — someone comments, replies to a story, or a follow-up comes due.
LinktoDM builds the message and puts it in the queue.
The queue releases messages at a steady rate rather than all at once.
Each one goes out and leaves the count.

Under normal traffic the whole trip takes seconds, which is why the queue is usually invisible: the count sits at 0 because messages leave as fast as they arrive. It becomes visible only when messages arrive faster than the safe rate lets them leave — the moment a post spikes — and that is exactly when you want it there.

Two kinds of waiting
Section titled “Two kinds of waiting”

Not everything in the queue is waiting for the same reason, which is why the queue panel counts them separately.

DMs are waiting on sending speed. They’re ready now; the queue is spacing them out. This is the number that moves during a spike.
Follow-ups are waiting on time. A follow-up step or a delay told them to go out later, and they sit in the queue until their timer says otherwise. A follow-up scheduled for tomorrow is in the queue all day, and that’s the feature working.
What the queue guarantees
Section titled “What the queue guarantees”

Nothing is dropped while it waits. A queued message is a message that will be sent, just not this second. It survives the wait, and the only things that remove it are being sent or being cleared by you.

It’s per account. The panel sits under the account switcher because the queue does too: every connected Instagram account or Facebook Page has its own, so a busy account and a quiet one don’t share a backlog.

The one thing the queue doesn’t do is go faster on request. There’s no priority lane and no setting to raise the rate; when Meta tightens, LinktoDM slows down deliberately so that the messages still get through.

Common questions
Section titled “Common questions”

Does the queue delay every DM? Technically yes, in practice no. Every message passes through it, but under normal traffic it’s out again in seconds. The delay only becomes noticeable when a post generates messages faster than the safe rate can release them.

Why does my queue say 0 when an automation is live? Because it’s keeping up. A count of 0 is the normal state, not a sign that nothing is firing. To confirm an automation is running, use its Hits column in the Automations list.

Can I make it send faster? No, and that’s the point. The rate is set by what the platform will accept from your account at that moment, not by a plan or a setting. The lever you do have is upstream: send fewer messages by tightening the trigger or by running fewer automations on the same account at once.

Will a queued message expire if it waits too long? No. Waiting doesn’t discard a message. It leaves the queue by being sent or by being cleared by you, and nothing else.

A follow-up is scheduled for next week — does it sit in the queue that whole time? Yes, and that’s expected. Follow-ups wait on their timer rather than on sending speed, so a large Follow-ups count on an account running long delays is normal.

Do my accounts share one queue? No. Every connected account has its own queue and its own rate, so a launch on one account doesn’t slow the others down.

Does pausing the queue switch my automations off? No. Triggers keep matching and messages keep piling up behind the pause — they’re delayed, not cancelled. To stop sending for longer than a few minutes, switch the automation off instead.

title: DM Rate Limits and Throttling
html:
DM Rate Limits and Throttling

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Meta decides how fast your account may send messages, not LinktoDM. Push past that line and the platform stops accepting messages — and an account that keeps pushing looks like spam, which is the more expensive problem of the two.

The rate shown in the queue panel therefore isn’t a fixed setting. It’s the speed LinktoDM has judged safe for your account at this moment.

Smart Queue Control

Section titled “Smart Queue Control”

The line under the queue panel — System will automatically reduce delivery speed during peak times — is the feature announcing itself, and Learn more beside it spells out the reasoning: when Instagram’s rate limits are hit, slowing messages down improves delivery success and avoids tripping spam detection.

In short, LinktoDM watches how the platform responds and eases off when it sees rate limiting, then picks the pace back up. Sending speed is adjusted for you, in both directions, and there is nothing to switch on.

The limits it’s working around

Section titled “The limits it’s working around”

The limits aren’t a secret — Meta publishes them in its Graph API rate limiting documentation. They’re worth knowing, because they explain why the queue behaves the way it does. The figures below are Instagram’s, which is where most LinktoDM automations run; Facebook Page messaging sits under the same system with its own numbers, and the queue treats both the same way. Instagram applies them per professional account, so every account you connect has its own budget:

What it covers Instagram’s limit
Your account’s total API activity 4,800 calls per 24 hours × the impressions your content earned in that window
DMs sent as a private reply to a comment on a post or reel 750 per hour
Private replies to comments on a Live 100 per second
DMs with text, links, reactions or stickers 100 per second
DMs carrying audio or video 10 per second

Two of those numbers do most of the work in practice.

The 24-hour budget moves with your reach. It’s a rolling window, and it’s multiplied by impressions — so a post that takes off raises your ceiling at the same time as it raises your volume, while a small account working through a backtracked week of comments has much less room than its follower count suggests.

Comment-to-DM automations meet the 750/hour wall first. The DM that answers a comment on a post or a reel is a private reply, and private replies are capped by the hour rather than by the second. A viral post generating thousands of qualifying comments in an hour is over that line no matter how the sending is spaced — which is exactly the case the queue is built for: it holds the surplus and keeps releasing it into the next hour instead of throwing it away.

When an account does cross a limit, Instagram answers with a throttling error (code 80002 for Instagram rate limits, or 4, 17, 32 and 613 depending on the token and the call) and reports how long access is restricted for. LinktoDM reads those responses and slows the queue rather than retrying into a closed door.

What that means in practice

Section titled “What that means in practice”

Slower is the safe outcome, not the failure. When the platform starts rate limiting, pushing harder gets messages rejected; easing off gets them delivered. A queue that drains slowly during a spike is the system choosing delivery over speed — the messages still arrive, a little later than they would have.

There’s nothing to configure. Throttling is automatic. There’s no setting to raise the rate, no way to buy more of it, and no priority lane for one message. The published limits are Instagram’s, and they apply to every tool that sends on your behalf.

Peak traffic is when it shows. A reel doing numbers, a launch, a giveaway — the hours when your automations are busiest are the hours the platform is strictest.

Sending fewer messages, not faster ones

Section titled “Sending fewer messages, not faster ones”

If the queue backs up further than you’re comfortable with, the lever is upstream of the queue:

  • Tighten the trigger so fewer comments qualify in the first place.
  • Run fewer automations on the same account at once, especially on posts that are live at the same time.
  • Cap the public replies with a per-post reply limit, which keeps a single post from generating an unbounded run of activity.
  • Be deliberate with backtracking: it answers a week of comments in one go, which lands in the queue as one burst — against an hourly private-reply limit that doesn’t care how old the comment is.

Rate limiting isn’t the same as an error

A slow queue is throttling working. A message that fails outright is something else — start with Instagram messaging API errors.

title: Check Your DM Queue Status
html:
Check Your DM Queue Status

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Click In queue in the console sidebar to expand the panel. Collapsed, it shows a single total; expanded, it breaks that total down and shows the rate messages are going out at.

What each number means

Section titled “What each number means”
  • The count beside In queue is everything waiting for this account, follow-ups and DMs together. It’s visible with the panel collapsed, so it works as a glance-check while you’re doing something else.
  • Follow-ups — messages scheduled for later by a follow-up step or a delay. These sit here until their timer is up, however long that is.
  • DMs — messages ready to send now, waiting only on sending speed.
  • 60 DMs/min is the rate the queue is releasing at right now. It isn’t fixed — see rate limits and throttling.

The two buttons beside the rate pause delivery and clear the queue.

Is a number here a problem?

Section titled “Is a number here a problem?”

Usually not. Read it as a rate, not a level — watch it for a minute and see which way it’s going.

  • Falling — the spike is draining. Nothing to do.
  • Holding steady on a busy post — messages are arriving about as fast as they’re going out. Also normal; it’ll drain when the comments slow down.
  • Sitting in Follow-ups and not moving — expected. Those are waiting on their schedule, not on the queue.
  • Climbing on an account with little traffic — worth a look. Check the queue isn’t paused first, since a paused queue fills without emptying, then work through Instagram automation not working.

A count of 0 while an automation is live is also normal, and the usual case: messages are leaving as fast as they arrive, so there’s never a backlog to show. To confirm an automation is actually firing, use its Hits column in the Automations list rather than the queue.

title: Pause, Clear or Cancel Queued DMs
html:
Pause, Clear or Cancel Queued DMs

3 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Two buttons sit beside the rate in the In queue panel: pause, which holds delivery, and the red clear, which empties the queue. They sound similar and are not — one delays messages, the other cancels them.

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to LinktoDM
  • The account whose queue you want with In queue expanded in the console sidebar

Pause delivery

Section titled “Pause delivery”

Click the pause button next to the rate. Delivery stops, and the panel says so until you start it again.

Press the green play button to resume. Everything that piled up meanwhile goes out from there.

Pausing stops delivery, not your automations. Triggers keep matching and messages keep landing in the queue behind the pause, so the count grows while it’s held — nothing is lost, it’s only late.

That makes pause the right control for a short, deliberate hold: you’ve spotted a typo in a published DM, or you’re mid-edit on an automation and don’t want the old version going out for the next few minutes. Fix the thing, then resume.

Don’t leave it paused

A paused queue is easy to forget about. Every comment that arrives meanwhile still queues up, and when you resume, all of it is due at once — the exact burst the queue exists to prevent. To stop sending for longer than a few minutes, switch the automation off instead.

Clear the queue

Section titled “Clear the queue”

The red trash button empties the queue. Everything waiting — DMs and scheduled follow-ups alike — is dropped and will not be sent.

Reach for it when the queue holds messages you actively don’t want delivered: a mistake published to a post that took off, or an automation that matched far more comments than you meant it to.

Two things to know before you press it:

  • It can’t be undone. A cleared message isn’t rescheduled or retried. The people waiting on it simply never hear back, and a comment that expected a DM goes unanswered.
  • It doesn’t switch anything off. Clearing empties what’s there right now. A live automation starts filling the queue again with the next comment, so if the automation itself is the problem, turn it off first and clear second — otherwise you’re clearing a queue that’s refilling behind you.

Which one you want

Section titled “Which one you want”
You want to Use
Hold messages for a few minutes and send them after Pause, then play
Stop one automation sending, permanently Switch that automation off
Keep the public replies but stop the DMs Disable the DM step
Cancel messages that are already waiting Clear (after switching the automation off)

You should now have

A queue you can hold and release on purpose — paused while you fix something, cleared when what’s waiting shouldn’t go out at all, and the automations behind it switched off first so it stays that way.
