title: Add another Instagram account
html:
Add another Instagram account

2 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Running more than one Instagram account — a personal brand and a shop, or several clients — means connecting each one to LinktoDM separately. The flow is the same one you used for your first account.

Before you begin

  • A LinktoDM account with at least one Instagram account already connected
  • Admin access to the Instagram account you are adding
  • For Facebook login: admin access to the Facebook Page you are adding

Add the account

Section titled “Add the account”
  1. Sign in at console.linktodm.com with your existing LinktoDM account.
  2. In the account rail down the left edge, click the + button. Your connected accounts are stacked above it.
  3. Choose Add Instagram account or Add Facebook page.
  4. Sign in to the account you are adding.
  5. Approve every permission it asks for, in particular messaging and comment access. A skipped permission is the usual reason an automation does nothing later.

Which login you pick is per account, not per LinktoDM login. Add Facebook page connects a Page you administer — enough on its own to automate Messenger DMs and comment-to-DM on Facebook posts, and if an Instagram account is linked to that Page it also brings the full Instagram feature set: Comment-to-DM, Story Replies, Click Tracking and Analytics. Add Instagram account is quicker and needs no Page. See Connect your Instagram account for the difference in full.

Switching between accounts

Section titled “Switching between accounts”

Connected accounts stack in the same left rail, and the name at the top of the sidebar tells you which one you are in. Automations, contacts and analytics all belong to the account currently selected — check it before building an automation, so the automation lands on the account you meant.

“Already linked to a different user”

Section titled ““Already linked to a different user””

An Instagram account can be connected to one LinktoDM account at a time. If you see this error, that Instagram account is still attached to another LinktoDM login — an old account of your own, or a teammate’s.

To move it, sign in to the LinktoDM account that currently holds it and remove it there, then add it again here. If that account is no longer needed at all, deleting it releases the link.

One automation tool at a time

This is separate from other apps like ManyChat. Meta lets only one app own a conversation, so an Instagram account still connected to another automation tool will not send DMs through LinktoDM even after it is added here. See Another app is controlling your conversations.

You should now have

A second Instagram account connected to the same LinktoDM login, with its own automations, and a switcher to move between them.

title: Limit Public Replies on an Instagram Automation
html:
Limit Public Replies on an Instagram Automation

2 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Public comment replies are the replies your automation leaves under the post, and they carry their own per-post limit — limit to 100 per post by default. On a post that suddenly does numbers, that ceiling is what keeps your comment section from filling with automated replies.

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to LinktoDM
  • An existing post, reel or story automation

Set the limit

Section titled “Set the limit”
  1. Open Automations in the console and open the automation you want to change.
  2. Find the Public comment reply row, under Post and Trigger.
  3. The toggle on the right turns public replies on and off. The dropdown beside it sets the cap — limit to 100 per post is the default.
  4. Pick the limit you want, then click Publish.

What number to pick

Section titled “What number to pick”

The 100 per post default covers a normal post comfortably. Raise it once you have watched an automation run cleanly, and raise it gradually rather than in one jump.

A brand new account going from zero to several thousand replies in an afternoon is the pattern platforms treat as spam, and the cost of that is your account, not the automation. The same caution applies to DM volume — 100 to 200 a day is the place to start.

Pair it with your trigger

The limit and the trigger solve different halves of the same problem. The trigger decides who gets a reply, the limit decides how many. On a giveaway with an Any Word trigger, the limit is the only thing standing between you and every comment on the post.

Public replies and DMs are separate

Section titled “Public replies and DMs are separate”

Turning the Public comment reply toggle off stops the visible replies under your post. The DM still goes out — that is set up further down the editor, under Setup direct message.

That split is useful: a giveaway can send everyone a DM without leaving a hundred identical comments on the post itself.

When an automation hits its limit

Section titled “When an automation hits its limit”

It stops leaving public replies on that post. The automation stays published and everything else about it is unchanged — raise the limit and it resumes.

If replies stopped and you did not expect it, this limit is the first thing to check, before anything in Automation not working.

You should now have

An automation that answers your commenters and stops at a number you chose, rather than running unbounded on a post that takes off overnight.

title: Backtrack Comments in an Automation
html:
Backtrack Comments in an Automation

3 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

An automation only sees comments posted after you publish it. So the usual story goes: a reel does numbers overnight, you set up an automation the next morning, and the two hundred comments that arrived while you were asleep sit there unanswered forever.

Backtracking fixes exactly that. It runs a published automation back over comments that are already on the post, up to 7 days old, and replies to the ones that match its trigger.

Before you begin

  • An account connected to LinktoDM
  • A post or reel automation that is published and switched on

Run a backtrack

Section titled “Run a backtrack”
  1. Open Automations in the console.
  2. Find the automation in the list and click the ··· menu at the end of its row.
  3. Choose Backtrack comments.
  1. The Backtrack comments dialog opens. Click Backtrack Now.
  1. Leave the dialog open until it finishes. It reports Status: Completed along with how many comments the run processed, and the time of the last backtrack.

Reading the result

Section titled “Reading the result”

Processed comments is how many comments the run looked at — the whole eligible history on the post, not the number of replies it sent.

To see how many actually matched, look at the Hits column for that automation back in the list. In the run above, 50 comments were processed and the automation picked up 4 hits: the other 46 didn’t match its trigger and were left alone, exactly as they would have been live.

Then check the post itself. Backtracked replies appear threaded under the original comment, however old it is — a comment from five days ago picks up its reply in the same place a live one would, rather than as a new comment at the bottom of the post.

That’s worth knowing before you run it: the replies land deep in the thread where they make sense in context, not stacked at the end where they’d read as a burst.

It respects the trigger you set

Section titled “It respects the trigger you set”

Backtracking doesn’t reply to everything it finds — it re-runs the automation’s own trigger over the old comments. Whatever the automation would have done live, it does now.

That includes Intent Match. The automation in this run had no keyword at all — just the description when asked about delay — and the backtrack still found the comments that meant that and skipped the rest.

Things worth knowing before you run it

Section titled “Things worth knowing before you run it”
  • 7 days is a hard edge. Comments older than that are out of reach, whatever you do. If a post is about to age past the window, backtrack it now.
  • The automation has to be on. A draft or a switched-off automation has no trigger to run, so there’s nothing to backtrack with.
  • Your public reply limit still applies. Backtracked replies count toward the per-post cap like any other. On a post with a long comment history, that cap is what stops a single backtrack from filling the whole thread at once.
  • Run it once per post. Comments already answered are skipped, but a second run still walks the history and costs you the wait for nothing.

Backtracking is a burst, not a trickle

A live automation replies as comments arrive, spread over hours. A backtrack answers a week of comments in one go, which is a much louder pattern from the platform’s side.

On a post with hundreds of old comments, keep your reply limit conservative for the first run rather than raising it and backtracking in the same sitting.

You should now have

A post that took off before your automation existed, answered anyway — every comment from the last 7 days checked against your trigger and replied to.

Section titled “What Happens After Deletion”

Once you confirm the deletion, you will be automatically logged out of your account. All your data, including automations, contact lists, and account settings, will be permanently removed from our database.

Need Help?

Section titled “Need Help?”

If you’re experiencing issues with your account or have concerns, please contact our support team before proceeding with account deletion. We’re here to help resolve any problems you may be facing.

title: Why an Instagram Professional Account Is Required
html:
Why an Instagram Professional Account Is Required

Updated Sep 9, 2026

LinktoDM cannot automate a personal Instagram account. Neither can any other tool, and the reason is not a limitation we chose.

Automation runs on an API, not on your login

Section titled “Automation runs on an API, not on your login”

LinktoDM does not sign in as you and click around Instagram. It talks to Meta’s official messaging API, which is the supported and policy-compliant way to send DMs and read comments on someone’s behalf.

That API is only available to Business and Creator accounts. Meta does not expose messaging or comment permissions on personal accounts at all, so there is nothing for LinktoDM to connect to. An automation built on a personal account would have no way to see a comment arrive or to send a reply.

Switching to a professional account is free, takes about a minute in the Instagram app, and does not change your handle, your followers or your posts.

Why Meta draws the line there

Section titled “Why Meta draws the line there”

A personal account is a person. A professional account is a business or a public figure who has accepted a different set of platform rules, including the ones covering automated messaging, rate limits and what may be sent in a DM.

Automated messaging is only permitted under that agreement. Tying the API to professional accounts is how Meta keeps automation inside a set of terms someone has actually agreed to, and how it can act against an account that abuses it.

What it means in practice

Section titled “What it means in practice”
  • Business and Creator both work. Pick whichever fits — Creator suits personal brands, Business suits shops and companies.
  • The account must stay professional. Switching back to personal cuts the connection, and your automations will stop.
  • This applies to Instagram automation only. If you are automating a Facebook Page — Messenger DMs and comment-to-DM on Facebook posts — you do not need an Instagram account at all, professional or otherwise.
  • Being professional is necessary but not always sufficient: the Facebook login path also wants the account linked to a Page, and some accounts are held back by other eligibility checks. See Why a Facebook Page is required and Instagram Messaging API Error.

Already professional and still blocked?

If your account is Business or Creator and the connection is still refused, it is usually an eligibility or permissions problem rather than an account-type one. Instagram Messaging API Error walks through the fix.

title: Why a Facebook Page Is Required
html:
Why a Facebook Page Is Required

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A Facebook Page is only required on one of the two ways into LinktoDM, and it buys you something. Here is what it is for, and when you can skip it.

The Page holds the permissions

Section titled “The Page holds the permissions”

On the Facebook login path, the permissions LinktoDM needs are not granted by an Instagram account. They are granted through the Facebook Page itself.

That Page is the object Meta attaches messaging and comment access to, and Page admins are the people allowed to grant it. This is why the connection asks you to be an admin of the Page: without that role there is nobody Meta will accept the grant from.

Because the Page carries the permissions, it is also enough on its own.

A Page by itself is enough

Section titled “A Page by itself is enough”

You do not need an Instagram account to use this path. Connect a Page you administer and LinktoDM automates the Page:

  • Messenger DMs
  • Comment-to-DM on your Facebook posts

That is a complete setup. Nothing has to be linked to Instagram for those automations to run.

Linking Instagram adds the Instagram features

Section titled “Linking Instagram adds the Instagram features”

Link an Instagram professional account to the same Page and the Page’s permissions extend to it, which is what unlocks:

  • Comment-to-DM automation on Instagram
  • Story replies
  • Click tracking
  • Analytics

An Instagram account with no linked Page cannot use this path — there is no Page to carry the permissions. That is the one thing the Page is genuinely required for.

When you do not need one

Section titled “When you do not need one”

Instagram login connects with your Instagram credentials alone. No Page, no Facebook account, no admin role — a good fit for creators and small brands who want automations running today and do not have a Page set up.

You keep the core of the product. Some of the features listed above depend on the Page-based permissions, so if click tracking or analytics matter to you, the Facebook path is the one to take. The full comparison is in Connect your Facebook account.

Choosing between them

Section titled “Choosing between them”
  • Only automate a Facebook Page — use Facebook login; Instagram is optional.
  • No Page today, want to start now — use Instagram login.
  • Page already set up, want everything — use Facebook login with your Instagram account linked to the Page.
  • Not sure — start with Instagram login. Connecting through Facebook later is a reconnection, not a rebuild.

Being an admin matters

Being able to post to a Page is not the same as administering it. If the connection fails part way through the Facebook flow, check your role on the Page before anything else.

You do not need an Instagram account to use this path. Connect a Page you administer and LinktoDM automates the Page:

Messenger DMs
Comment-to-DM on your Facebook posts

That is a complete setup. Nothing has to be linked to Instagram for those automations to run.

Only automate a Facebook Page — use Facebook login; Instagram is optional.
No Page today, want to start now — use Instagram login.
Page already set up, want everything — use Facebook login with your Instagram account linked to the Page.

The LinktoDM Zapier Integration

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Your automations already collect the things a business actually runs on — an email, a phone number, a plan tier, a tag that marks someone as ready to buy. Until now that lived in LinktoDM and left as a CSV. Zapier is how it reaches the rest of your stack the second it’s captured: Google Sheets, Notion, Airtable, Mailchimp, HubSpot, Slack, Twilio, Calendly, Shopify, and thousands more.

LinktoDM is the trigger, your other app is the action

Section titled “LinktoDM is the trigger, your other app is the action”

The integration works in one direction. LinktoDM starts Zaps; it doesn’t receive them.

So “a contact hands over their email in a DM” can become a row in a sheet, a subscriber in Mailchimp, and a Slack message — but Zapier can’t reach back in to send a DM for you. Sending stays in your flows.

Six events, all instant

Section titled “Six events, all instant”

Every one is instant: it fires on a webhook the moment the event happens, rather than waiting for Zapier to poll on a schedule. The gap between a comment landing and your Zap running is seconds, which is the difference between following up while someone is still holding their phone and following up tomorrow.

Event Fires when
New Contact Someone interacts with one of your automations for the first time
New or Updated Email A contact’s email is captured or changed
New or Updated Phone Number A contact’s phone number is captured or changed
New Tagged Contact A tag is added to a contact
Contact Tag Removed A tag is removed from a contact
New or Updated Custom Field A custom field value is set or changed

What you can build

Section titled “What you can build”

The obvious version is “copy the email into a sheet”. These are the ones worth the setup time.

A contact sheet that keeps itself current. Google Sheets has a Lookup Spreadsheet Row action with a create the row if it doesn’t exist yet option. Look the contact up by username, then update. Point all six triggers at the same sheet and each person gets one row that fills in over time — email in column C when they hand it over, plan_tier in column E when it changes — instead of six lists you have to reconcile.

One digest instead of two hundred pings. Digest by Zapier collects entries and releases them on a schedule — daily, weekly, monthly, or once a set number have piled up. Point New Contact at it and a reel that goes off overnight becomes one summary at 9am rather than a Slack channel nobody can read.

Speed-to-lead on phone numbers. New or Updated Phone Number → Twilio → an SMS with your booking link, inside a minute of them typing it. For anything high-ticket this is the single highest-leverage Zap on the list: the number came from a DM conversation, so they’re expecting you.

Sell without a checkout page. A flow’s payment node clears → it adds a course-paid tag → Zapier invites them to your Circle or Discord community, raises the invoice in QuickBooks, and adds them to the onboarding sequence. The buyer never leaves Instagram.

Access that ends by itself. The mirror image, and the one people forget. A flow removes subscription-active → Zapier revokes the community seat, unshares the Drive folder, logs the churn. Built as a pair with the one above, membership follows the tag in both directions and nobody has to remember.

Route by tag instead of building five Zaps. Paths splits one Zap into as many as ten branches on conditions you set, so a single New Tagged Contact Zap can send vip to your CRM, refund-requested to a support queue, and webinar-yes to Calendly.

Quiz answers you can actually read. A flow that stores replies with Set user field turns a DM quiz into research: every answer lands in a sheet, already attached to the person who gave it.

Where to go next

Section titled “Where to go next”

Connect LinktoDM to Zapier takes about a minute, then build your first Zap walks through one end to end — starting with the LinktoDM automation that creates the contacts in the first place.

Some Zapier tools need a paid Zapier plan

Filters work on every plan. Paths needs Zapier’s Professional tier or above, and Digest has its own storage limits. Nothing here changes what LinktoDM sends — only what Zapier can do with it once it arrives.

title: Connect LinktoDM to Zapier
html:
Connect LinktoDM to Zapier

3 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

LinktoDM’s Zapier integration is currently in private beta, so it won’t turn up if you search for it in Zapier’s app directory on its own. You accept an invite link once to unlock it — after that, LinktoDM behaves like any other app in your Zap editor, and you only connect your account once.

Accept the invite

Section titled “Accept the invite”

  1. Open the invite link: zapier.com/developer/public-invite/245216/f0fee79ca6bcee09181f79f9b4f16fd1.

  2. Click Accept Invite & Build a Zap.

    Zapier flags that the app “has not been reviewed or approved by Zapier for functionality or security” — that’s standard for anything still in private beta, not a sign something’s wrong. Accepting just unlocks the app for your Zapier account.

  3. Accepting takes you to your Zapier dashboard — you’ll land on the Zap workflows page. Click + Create to start a new Zap.

Add your account

Section titled “Add your account”

  1. In the Zap editor’s trigger step, search for LinktoDM and select it as your trigger app. It shows up tagged Invite Only — that tag is expected and just means the app hasn’t gone public on Zapier yet.

  2. Pick a Trigger event — any of the six will do while you’re connecting, and New Contact is the simplest.

  3. Under Account, click Sign in. Zapier first confirms you want to link this app:

  4. Click Connect. Zapier opens a LinktoDM window in your browser.

  5. Sign in with the account you use at console.linktodm.com and click Allow access on LinktoDM’s consent screen. If you manage more than one Instagram account, pick the one this connection should cover.

  6. Back in Zapier, your account name appears under Account and Continue becomes available. That’s the connection done — future Zaps just pick this account from the dropdown instead of repeating steps 3–5.

Zapier only sees what this account can see

The connection inherits the permissions of the LinktoDM account you signed in with, and nothing more. Remove it whenever you like from Zapier’s My Apps page — Zaps using it stop firing immediately, and nothing in LinktoDM changes.

Connect a second account

Section titled “Connect a second account”

One connection covers one LinktoDM account. To automate a second Instagram account, click Change next to Account in any Zap, choose Connect a new account, and sign in with that one. Zapier keeps both and lets you pick per Zap, so name them clearly — the account label is the only thing telling them apart later.

If it doesn’t connect

Section titled “If it doesn’t connect”

LinktoDM doesn’t show up when I search for it in Zapier. You haven’t accepted the invite yet — go back to Accept the invite above.

The sign-in window doesn’t open. Pop-up blockers swallow it. Allow pop-ups for zapier.com and click Sign in again.

“401 Unauthorized” on a Zap that used to work. The connection was removed or the session expired. Reconnect the account from Zapier’s My Apps page; your Zaps keep their configuration.

Still stuck? Email support@linktodm.com with the Zap name and the trigger you’re using. We usually reply the same business day.

title: LinktoDM Trigger Events in Zapier
html:
LinktoDM Trigger Events in Zapier

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Six trigger events are live. Every one is instant — it fires on a webhook the moment the event happens in LinktoDM, so nothing waits on a polling interval.

Trigger Fires when Try it for
New Contact Someone interacts with one of your automations for the first time Logging every lead as it arrives
New or Updated Email A contact’s email is captured or changed Starting an email sequence
New or Updated Phone Number A contact’s phone number is captured or changed WhatsApp or SMS follow-up
New Tagged Contact A tag is added to a contact Segment-triggered onboarding
Contact Tag Removed A tag is removed from a contact Churn and revoking access
New or Updated Custom Field A custom field value is set or changed Tier changes, codes, preferences

New Contact

Section titled “New Contact”

The widest net there is. LinktoDM creates a contact the first time someone interacts with any published automation — a comment on a post automation, a story reply, a DM that matches a flow trigger — and this event fires on that moment. Every automation you run feeds it, so it’s the trigger to reach for when you want everything recorded.

Because it depends on an automation existing, it’s worth setting up in that order: build your first Zap walks through the LinktoDM half first. Note that it fires once per person — later interactions update the existing contact instead.

Send it to a Google Sheet or a Notion database and you have a lead log that builds itself. Or point it at Slack, so the reel going viral at 2am arrives as a channel message with the username attached instead of as a surprise the next morning.

New or Updated Email and New or Updated Phone Number

Section titled “New or Updated Email and New or Updated Phone Number”

These two fire when a collected email or phone number lands on a contact, or when a value that was already there changes. Both compare against what LinktoDM already held, so re-saving the same value does nothing.

They get their own page: Sync email and phone updates to Zapier.

New Tagged Contact and Contact Tag Removed

Section titled “New Tagged Contact and Contact Tag Removed”

Tags are how a flow says “this specific thing just happened” to the rest of your stack. Both triggers fire from the Add contact tag and Remove contact tag actions in your flows, and the added tag’s name travels with the event.

They get their own page, with the flow side included: Trigger Zaps when contact tags are added or removed.

New or Updated Custom Field

Section titled “New or Updated Custom Field”

Custom fields hold values rather than labels, so this trigger carries the most detail — including the field’s previous value alongside the new one. You pick which field to watch when you set the trigger up, so it’s one Zap per field.

See Sync custom field changes to Zapier.

What every trigger hands you

Section titled “What every trigger hands you”

Each event arrives with the whole contact attached, not just the value that changed — username, name, email, phone number, the previous value, the platform user ID, the event type, and a timestamp. Anything in this panel can be dropped into any field of your action.

Because the username travels with every event, you can keep one row per contact in a sheet or one record per contact in your CRM and have all six triggers write to the same place, rather than scattering one person across six lists.

title: Build Your First LinktoDM Zap
html:
Build Your First LinktoDM Zap

4 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

A Zap on New Contact fires when LinktoDM creates a contact. So this walkthrough has two halves, and the first one is the half people skip: getting LinktoDM to produce contacts at all. A Zap that “never fires” is usually a Zap whose LinktoDM side was never doing anything.

We’ll publish an automation, watch a real contact appear in Contacts, and only then wire up Zapier.

Before you begin

  • LinktoDM connected to Zapier
  • An Instagram post or reel you can attach an automation to
  • A second Instagram account that has never messaged you, to test with

Contacts come from your automations

Section titled “Contacts come from your automations”

You never add contacts by hand. LinktoDM creates one the first time somebody interacts with any automation you’ve published — and after that, every interaction updates the record it already has. That covers:

  • a comment on a post or reel automation
  • a story reply or reaction
  • a DM that matches a flow trigger
  • any step further into a flow, like a button tap

A contact is the person plus everything you’ve learned about them: username, when they last interacted, and any email, phone number, tags or custom fields your automations have collected.

1. Publish an automation

Section titled “1. Publish an automation”

Any published automation will do. If you already have one running, skip ahead — it’s already creating contacts.

title: Sync Email and Phone Updates to Zapier
html:
Sync Email and Phone Updates to Zapier

Updated Sep 9, 2026

An email address or a phone number is the one thing a DM conversation gives you that outlives the DM. New or Updated Email and New or Updated Phone Number are how it leaves LinktoDM the moment it arrives, instead of waiting for someone to export a CSV on Friday.

Both are driven by the Collect email and Collect phone steps in your automations: the contact answers in the thread, LinktoDM validates and saves the value, and the Zap fires.

New or Updated Email

Section titled “New or Updated Email”

Map Email into the action and the address flows through.

The obvious pairing is your email tool — Mailchimp, ConvertKit, Klaviyo — so the lead magnet someone asked for in a comment reaches their inbox before they’ve closed Instagram. Worth building:

  • Deliver, then nurture. Add the subscriber to a list and let your existing welcome sequence do the rest. The DM promised the thing; the sequence keeps the conversation going after Instagram is closed.
  • A list you own. Append every address to a sheet or Airtable base alongside the username, so your audience isn’t only reachable through one platform’s algorithm.
  • Bounce recovery. An update is a signal in itself. A contact correcting their address usually means the first one bounced — send updates to a “re-check these” view and you’ll catch the ones your email tool quietly gave up on.

New or Updated Phone Number

Section titled “New or Updated Phone Number”

The same shape, for phone numbers.

This is the trigger high-ticket sellers get the most from. Someone who hands over a phone number in a DM is a warmer lead than someone who hands over an email, and a Zap that texts them a booking link inside a minute converts very differently from one that emails them tomorrow.

  • SMS or WhatsApp confirmation. Twilio or your WhatsApp provider, sending the booking link while they’re still in the app.
  • A call list that sorts itself. A sheet row per number with the username and timestamp, so your team works down warm leads in the order they arrived.
  • Straight into the CRM. Create or update the contact in HubSpot or Pipedrive with the Instagram handle attached, so whoever picks up the call knows where the lead came from.

Both triggers only fire on a real change

Re-saving the same value does nothing — LinktoDM compares against what it already held. So a contact who runs through your automation five times doesn’t produce five identical rows, and you don’t need a Zapier filter to deduplicate.

Ask for the country code

Section titled “Ask for the country code”

The Collect phone step’s retry message exists to enforce this, and it matters more once Zapier is involved: a number without a country code is ambiguous, and an SMS tool downstream will either reject it or send it somewhere unexpected. Show a formatted example in both the ask and the retry and most failures disappear before they reach your Zap.

A DM answer isn't marketing consent

Someone answering “what’s your email?” in a DM has not opted into a newsletter, and a Zap that adds them to one on their behalf doesn’t change that. Say where the address is going in the ask itself, and keep whatever record your local rules require.

One automation, both triggers

Section titled “One automation, both triggers”

An automation that collects both fires both triggers, one after the other, as the contact answers each question — so two separate Zaps can send each value exactly where it belongs without either knowing about the other.

title: Sync Custom Field Changes to Zapier
html:
Sync Custom Field Changes to Zapier

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Custom fields hold actual values on a contact — a plan tier, a discount code, a preferred language — rather than the yes/no labels that tags give you. New or Updated Custom Field fires whenever one of those values is set or changed, which makes it the most detailed trigger the integration has.

One Zap watches one field

Section titled “One Zap watches one field”

Unlike the other triggers, this one asks a question on the Configure tab: which field? The dropdown lists every custom field on your account, and the Zap only fires for the one you choose.

So watching three fields means three Zaps. That sounds like duplication, and it’s actually the useful part: a plan_tier change and a preferred_language change should almost never do the same thing downstream, and separate Zaps let you send them separate places without a filter step.

The field has to exist before the Zap can watch it

The dropdown reads your live LinktoDM fields. If the one you want isn’t there, create it first — the Set user field action in a flow has a + Create new field button — then hit Refresh in the Zapier dropdown.

Mapping the value

Section titled “Mapping the value”

On the action side it behaves like any other trigger: click a field, pick Custom Field from the LinktoDM step, and the value flows through.

Previous value is the interesting part

Section titled “Previous value is the interesting part”

The payload carries the field’s previous value next to the new one. That’s what turns this from a sync into something you can act on, because the change is usually the story rather than the number.

  • Tier upgrades. Watch plan_tier and post “Priya moved silver → gold” into your sales channel. Both halves of that sentence come from the one event, and a Zapier filter on the previous value lets you treat an upgrade differently from a downgrade.
  • Codes and coupons. Watch a discount_code field, have Zapier create the matching coupon in Shopify, and write the result back to the contact.
  • Routing. Watch preferred_language and assign the conversation to the right person on your team in Intercom or HubSpot.
  • Quiz and survey answers. A flow that stores an answer with Set user field can hand every response straight to a sheet, so a DM quiz doubles as research you can actually read.
  • An audit trail. Append every change to a log sheet — field, old value, new value, timestamp — and you can answer “when did this contact become a customer?” months later.

A no-op save still counts as a change here

Unlike the email and phone triggers, this one is about the field being set, so writing the same value again can fire it. If your flow re-saves a field on every message, put a condition in front of the Set user field action, or add a Zapier filter comparing the value to the previous one.

A flow and a Zap, together

Section titled “A flow and a Zap, together”

The flow decides who qualifies and the Zap does the paperwork. Neither needs to know about the other, which is why you can change the flow’s wording ten times without touching the Zap.

title: Trigger Zaps When Contact Tags Are Added or Removed
html:
Trigger Zaps When Contact Tags Are Added or Removed

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A tag is the cleanest way for a flow to say “this specific thing just happened” to the rest of your stack. Two triggers listen for it — New Tagged Contact when one is added, Contact Tag Removed when one comes off — and between them they cover granting something and taking it away.

Tags come from your flows

Section titled “Tags come from your flows”

Neither trigger fires on its own. Both are driven by the Add contact tag and Remove contact tag actions in a flow, so the flow is where you decide who qualifies. Add an Action node, then pick the action type.

Add contact tag takes a list of tags rather than one. Type a tag and press Enter to add it; anything already on the contact is left alone.

Because a single action can apply several tags, it produces one event per tag. A Zap watching for vip won’t be confused by newsletter arriving in the same breath, but a Zap that reacts to any tag will run twice — filter on Tag Name if that matters.

That split between flow and Zap is the point. The flow holds the logic and can change as often as you like; the Zap only cares that a named tag moved. Rewrite the DM copy, add a condition, swap the trigger keyword — the Zap keeps working untouched.

Name tags after the state, not the campaign

webinar-yes still reads correctly next March. march-webinar-signup-final doesn’t, and you’ll be rebuilding the Zap when the next one runs. Tags that name a state survive campaigns; tags that name a campaign don’t.

New Tagged Contact

Section titled “New Tagged Contact”

The added tag’s name comes through in the payload, so one Zap can serve several tags — map Tag Name into the action and use a Zapier filter or paths to route on it.

What people wire it to:

  • Bookings. A flow tags call-requested when someone picks that button in a DM → Zapier creates the Calendly invite and emails the link.
  • Paid community access. Tag course-paid after a payment node clears → Zapier invites them to Circle, Discord or a shared Notion space.
  • CRM stages. Tag qualified → the deal moves to the next stage in HubSpot or Pipedrive, with the Instagram username on the record so your team knows where the lead came from.
  • Waitlists. Tag vip-waitlist → a row in a sheet you can sort, count and export when the product opens.
  • Fulfilment. Tag sample-requested → a shipping label task in Trello or Asana, no one retyping an address.

Contact Tag Removed

Section titled “Contact Tag Removed”

The mirror image, and the one people forget to build. Removing a tag is how access ends, and it’s worth automating for the same reason granting it is — the manual version gets skipped.

  • Revoke on churn. A flow strips subscription-active → Zapier removes them from the paid community, unshares the Drive folder, and appends a line to a churn log.
  • Win-backs. trial coming off a contact is the cue to start the win-back sequence in your email tool.
  • Keeping lists honest. Removing newsletter in LinktoDM unsubscribes them in Mailchimp too, so the two never disagree about who opted out.

Both directions, one system

Section titled “Both directions, one system”

Built as a pair, membership follows the tag automatically in both directions, and the tag on the contact is a reliable answer to “does this person have access?” — because it’s the same fact both Zaps are reading.

Test revocation before you trust it

A revoking Zap acts on a real account in a real app. Run it against your own second Instagram account first and confirm what it removes, because a Zap wired to the wrong tag will happily lock out paying customers.

text:
Trigger Zaps When Contact Tags Are Added or Removed

Updated Sep 9, 2026

A tag is the cleanest way for a flow to say “this specific thing just happened” to the rest of your stack. Two triggers listen for it — New Tagged Contact when one is added, Contact Tag Removed when one comes off — and between them they cover granting something and taking it away.

Tags come from your flows
Section titled “Tags come from your flows”

Neither trigger fires on its own. Both are driven by the Add contact tag and Remove contact tag actions in a flow, so the flow is where you decide who qualifies. Add an Action node, then pick the action type.

Add contact tag and Remove contact tag are the two that drive these triggers

Add contact tag takes a list of tags rather than one. Type a tag and press Enter to add it; anything already on the contact is left alone.

One action can apply several tags — each one fires New Tagged Contact

Because a single action can apply several tags, it produces one event per tag. A Zap watching for vip won’t be confused by newsletter arriving in the same breath, but a Zap that reacts to any tag will run twice — filter on Tag Name if that matters.

The same node, configured to remove a tag — this is what fires Contact Tag Removed

That split between flow and Zap is the point. The flow holds the logic and can change as often as you like; the Zap only cares that a named tag moved. Rewrite the DM copy, add a condition, swap the trigger keyword — the Zap keeps working untouched.

Name tags after the state, not the campaign

webinar-yes still reads correctly next March. march-webinar-signup-final doesn’t, and you’ll be rebuilding the Zap when the next one runs. Tags that name a state survive campaigns; tags that name a campaign don’t.

New Tagged Contact
Section titled “New Tagged Contact”

The added tag’s name comes through in the payload, so one Zap can serve several tags — map Tag Name into the action and use a Zapier filter or paths to route on it.

The tag's own name is part of the event, so the Zap knows which tag fired

What people wire it to:

Bookings. A flow tags call-requested when someone picks that button in a DM → Zapier creates the Calendly invite and emails the link.
Paid community access. Tag course-paid after a payment node clears → Zapier invites them to Circle, Discord or a shared Notion space.
CRM stages. Tag qualified → the deal moves to the next stage in HubSpot or Pipedrive, with the Instagram username on the record so your team knows where the lead came from.
Waitlists. Tag vip-waitlist → a row in a sheet you can sort, count and export when the product opens.
Fulfilment. Tag sample-requested → a shipping label task in Trello or Asana, no one retyping an address.
Contact Tag Removed
Section titled “Contact Tag Removed”

The mirror image, and the one people forget to build. Removing a tag is how access ends, and it’s worth automating for the same reason granting it is — the manual version gets skipped.

Contact Tag Removed carries the contact, so the Zap knows whose access to revoke
Revoke on churn. A flow strips subscription-active → Zapier removes them from the paid community, unshares the Drive folder, and appends a line to a churn log.
Win-backs. trial coming off a contact is the cue to start the win-back sequence in your email tool.
Keeping lists honest. Removing newsletter in LinktoDM unsubscribes them in Mailchimp too, so the two never disagree about who opted out.
Both directions, one system
Section titled “Both directions, one system”
Flow: payment clears → Add tag (course-paid)    → Zap: invite to community
Flow: refund issued  → Remove tag (course-paid) → Zap: revoke community access

Built as a pair, membership follows the tag automatically in both directions, and the tag on the contact is a reliable answer to “does this person have access?” — because it’s the same fact both Zaps are reading.

Test revocation before you trust it

A revoking Zap acts on a real account in a real app. Run it against your own second Instagram account first and confirm what it removes, because a Zap wired to the wrong tag will happily lock out paying customers.

title: Connect LinktoDM to Claude
html:
Connect LinktoDM to Claude

Updated Sep 9, 2026

LinktoDM ships a hosted MCP server (Model Context Protocol) so any MCP-compatible AI client (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, and others) can read your LinktoDM account, contacts, automations, and analytics, and act on your behalf. Connection takes about a minute and uses your existing LinktoDM login (OAuth), with no API keys to copy or rotate.

The MCP URL

Section titled “The MCP URL”

Every client uses the same URL. Copy it once and paste it where the client asks for the server endpoint.

Authentication is handled automatically over OAuth. When the client first connects, you’ll be sent to a LinktoDM sign-in page in your browser to approve access.

The AI only sees what your account can see

Permissions follow your existing LinktoDM role, and you can revoke access at any time from console.linktodm.com → Settings → Connected apps.

Set up Claude

Section titled “Set up Claude”

  1. Open Claude and go to Settings → Connectors.

  2. Click Add custom connector.

  3. Enter LinktoDM as the name and paste the MCP URL into the Server URL field.

  4. Click Connect. Claude opens a LinktoDM sign-in page in your browser. Sign in with the account you use at console.linktodm.com and approve the requested permissions.

  5. Back in Claude, LinktoDM appears as a connected source. Start a new chat and ask something like “How many automations did I run last week?”

On Claude Desktop the same Settings → Connectors flow applies on recent versions. If your version doesn’t show that menu, update Claude Desktop or use claude.ai in the browser.

What you can do once connected

Section titled “What you can do once connected”

Whatever the client lets you do in natural language. Common asks:

  • “List my LinktoDM automations and which ones are active.”
  • “How many DMs did my comment-to-DM automations send last week?”
  • “Show me the latest contacts that opted in to my list.”
  • “Pause the automation for my last reel.”
  • “Export my conversion analytics for the past 30 days as CSV.”

Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

“401 Unauthorized” after connecting

Section titled ““401 Unauthorized” after connecting”

The OAuth token expired or was revoked. In the client, disconnect the LinktoDM server and reconnect. You’ll be sent through the sign-in flow again.

Client says “could not connect to server”

Section titled “Client says “could not connect to server””

Confirm you copied the full URL (it ends with /v1/mcp/). If you’re behind a corporate proxy, allow outbound HTTPS to https://api.linktodm.com/v1/mcp/.

Tools aren’t showing up in the chat

Section titled “Tools aren’t showing up in the chat”

Most clients require you to explicitly enable the connector for the conversation. Claude: toggle the connector chip; ChatGPT: enable it in the connector menu; Cursor and VS Code: switch to Agent mode. Check the client’s MCP panel to confirm the server shows as connected before asking the AI to use it.

Sign-in page doesn’t open

Section titled “Sign-in page doesn’t open”

Pop-up blockers can swallow the OAuth window. Allow pop-ups for the AI client’s domain and try again.

Still stuck?

Section titled “Still stuck?”

Email us at support@linktodm.com with the client name, the version, and a screenshot of the error. We usually reply the same business day.

Thanks, that helps us prioritise.

title: Disconnect ManyChat from Your Instagram Account
html:
Disconnect ManyChat from Your Instagram Account

1 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Instagram lets one app run messaging on an account at a time, so ManyChat has to let go of yours before LinktoDM can take over. That takes two removals: take the account out of ManyChat, then withdraw the permission Instagram is still holding for it.

Before you begin

  • Access to the ManyChat account that currently holds your Instagram account
  • Admin access to the Instagram account you're moving
  • Your ManyChat automations copied or screenshotted, ready to rebuild here

Remove the Instagram account inside ManyChat

Section titled “Remove the Instagram account inside ManyChat”

In ManyChat, go to Settings, then Instagram under Channels in the middle column. Scroll to the bottom of that page and you’ll find three options together — Refresh Instagram Permissions, Disable Instagram Channel, and Remove Instagram Account from Manychat.

Disable is the temporary one; it pauses the channel and can be switched back on. You want Remove.

ManyChat then asks you to confirm, and it means it: tick both acknowledgements, type Remove in the box, and click Confirm. The dialog tells you how many Instagram contacts you’re about to lose.

Remove ManyChat from Instagram’s app list

Section titled “Remove ManyChat from Instagram’s app list”

Instagram keeps its own list of connected apps, and removing the channel inside ManyChat doesn’t touch it. On the Instagram mobile app, open your profile, tap the ☰ menu, then Settings and activity. Scroll down to App website permissions and choose Apps and websites.

On the Active tab, tap Remove next to Manychat-IG and confirm. Ours is on this list too, as LinktoDM or as Salesmorph — leave that one where it is.

You should now have

Your Instagram account removed from ManyChat, and ManyChat gone from Instagram’s own Apps and websites list.

title: Disconnect ManyChat from Facebook
html:
Disconnect ManyChat from Facebook

4 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

Facebook holds two separate connections, in two separate places: a business integration on your profile, and a connected app on your Page. Clearing the first doesn’t clear the second, and the second is the one that decides which app may act on your conversations.

Before you begin

  • Admin access to the Facebook profile the Instagram account sits under
  • Admin access to the Facebook Page it is linked to

Remove the ManyChat business integration

Section titled “Remove the ManyChat business integration”

Start on your personal profile. On facebook.com, open the profile menu at the top-right, then Settings & privacy → Settings. In the left column, under Your activity, choose Business integrations. The Active tab lists every app connected to your account — click Remove next to Manychat, confirm, then Done.

Ours is on that list too, as LinktoDM or as Salesmorph — both are us. Remove only Manychat and leave ours alone.

Facebook offers to notify ManyChat that you removed it. Whether you tick that makes no difference to the connection itself.

Strip ManyChat’s control on your Page

Section titled “Strip ManyChat’s control on your Page”

Business integrations is a permission you granted from your profile; Connected Apps is what currently has messaging access to the Page. This is the list that still holds ManyChat after everything else looks clean.

  1. On facebook.com, open the profile menu top-right and switch into your Page profile. These settings don’t exist on your personal profile.
  2. Go to Settings & privacy → Settings, then Page setup in the left column.
  3. Scroll down to Advanced messaging — manage your advanced messaging settings — and open it.
  4. Connected Apps lists every app with messaging access, each with its App ID and an Edit button: The following apps are currently connected to your Page.

Read the list. Anything with -IG after its name is an Instagram messaging app, and each one you don’t recognise is a candidate for the app that’s holding your conversations — Manychat-IG here, but also any trial you signed up for and forgot.

Removing the business integration above usually clears ManyChat’s row from this list on its own, though it can take a few minutes to catch up. So check here after you’ve done that step, not before.

If Manychat-IG is still listed, there’s no Remove button on this screen — what you can do instead is take away its ability to seize your conversations. Click Edit next to it. The dialog has two toggles under Messenger permissions and the same two again under Instagram permissions:

Toggle What it grants
Access standby channel The app can view conversation events, even when it isn’t the thread owner
Take control of conversations The app can take control of conversations from other apps

Switch Take control of conversations off in both halves, then Save. That’s the toggle that decides who owns a thread — left on, ManyChat can reclaim conversations after you’ve moved.

Do the same for any other -IG app you’re not using. You’ll come back to this screen later to confirm LinktoDM’s are switched on, which is the same dialog read the other way round.

Clear ManyChat as the default routing app

Section titled “Clear ManyChat as the default routing app”

The default routing app decides which app receives and replies to your messages, and it’s the setting most migrations never touch — everything else can be correct while your Page still routes conversations somewhere else.

From the same Page setup screen, open Instagram conversation routing (and Messenger conversation routing if you automate your Facebook Page too). Look at Default routing app — the app that will receive and reply to messages by default.

If ManyChat is named there, clear it: click the ··· menu and choose Remove. You’ll set LinktoDM in its place once it’s connected, from this same menu’s Edit.

Routing paths below it can stay empty — No routing paths is the normal state, and those are for directing specific messaging links or ad campaigns to different apps.

You should now have

ManyChat removed from your Facebook profile’s business integrations, stripped of control on your Page’s Connected Apps list, and no longer your Page’s default routing app. Nothing is holding the account.

Next: Migrate your connection

title: Connect Your Instagram Account to LinktoDM
html:
Connect Your Instagram Account to LinktoDM

2 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

With ManyChat removed from Instagram and Facebook, the account is free. Connecting it to LinktoDM is the ordinary connection flow — the only question is which screen you start from.

Before you begin

  • ManyChat removed from Instagram, from Facebook business integrations, and from your Page's Connected Apps
  • Admin access to the Instagram account you're connecting
  • For the Facebook login: admin access to the Page that account is linked to

If you’re new to LinktoDM

Section titled “If you’re new to LinktoDM”

Sign up at console.linktodm.com and the connection screen is the first thing you see. Pick Continue with Instagram or Continue with Facebook, sign in with the account you just freed from ManyChat, and say yes to every permission — messaging and comment access above all, because that’s what your automations run on.

If you already have a LinktoDM account

Section titled “If you already have a LinktoDM account”

You don’t need a second login. Click the + in the account rail down the left edge of the dashboard, choose Add Instagram account or Add Facebook page, and you’ll land on the same sign-in flow. The new account joins the rail alongside the one you already have.

Connected accounts stack in that rail, and the name at the top of the sidebar tells you which one you’re in. Automations, contacts and analytics all belong to the account currently selected — worth a glance before you start rebuilding, so your work lands on the account you meant.

Which login to pick

Section titled “Which login to pick”

The two buttons aren’t interchangeable, and it’s worth a minute to choose:

  • Connect your Instagram account is the short path — no Facebook Page, no Business portfolio, just your Instagram credentials.
  • Connect your Facebook account takes a Page you administer and unlocks the fuller feature set, plus Messenger and Facebook comment automation if you want them.

Coming from ManyChat you already have the Facebook Page linkage it required, so the Facebook path costs you nothing extra. LinktoDM doesn’t need it, though — either route works, and the choice is per account rather than per login.

“Already linked to a different user”

An Instagram account can be connected to one LinktoDM account at a time. If you see this, that account is still attached to another LinktoDM login — an old account of your own, or a teammate’s. Add another Instagram account explains how to release it.

You should now have

The Instagram account you moved off ManyChat now connected to LinktoDM, with messaging and comment permissions approved and the account showing in the account rail.

Next: Verify it's gone

title: Verify the Switch from ManyChat to LinktoDM
html:
Verify the Switch from ManyChat to LinktoDM

4 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

ManyChat is gone and LinktoDM is connected. This is where you confirm the switch actually landed, because a removal that looked successful in one place is routinely still live in another, and the only symptom is a DM that never sends.

Five checks. The first three are lists that should now show LinktoDM and nothing else; the last two are settings that decide whether it can act.

1. Facebook: Business integrations

Section titled “1. Facebook: Business integrations”

Settings & privacy → Settings → Your activity → Business integrations.

The Active tab should count 1 and list only ours — LinktoDM or Salesmorph, both are us. ManyChat should have moved to the Removed tab; seeing it there is the positive confirmation, not just its absence from Active.

2. Facebook Page: Connected Apps

Section titled “2. Facebook Page: Connected Apps”

3. Instagram: Apps and websites

Section titled “3. Instagram: Apps and websites”

Settings and activity → App website permissions → Apps and websites, on the Active tab. On desktop it’s at instagram.com/accounts/manage_access.

Instagram hands messaging to a single app. An entry still sitting on any of the three lists keeps ManyChat as the thread owner, and your LinktoDM automation will post the public reply and then fail on the DM with no visible error. Don’t move on until all three lists are clear.

Section titled “4. LinktoDM’s Page permissions”

Back on the Page’s Connected Apps — Settings & privacy → Settings → Page setup → Advanced messaging — click Edit next to LinktoDM. This is the dialog you used to switch ManyChat’s control off, read the other way round.

All four toggles should be on: Access standby channel and Take control of conversations, once under Messenger permissions and again under Instagram permissions.

With Take control of conversations off, everything else on this page can be correct and your DMs still won’t send.

Section titled “5. LinktoDM is the default routing app”

Still under Page setup, open Instagram conversation routing (and Messenger conversation routing if you automate your Facebook Page too). Under Default routing app, click the ··· menu, choose Edit, pick LinktoDM from the App dropdown, and Save.

Routing paths below it can stay empty — No routing paths is the normal state, and those are for directing specific messaging links or ad campaigns to different apps.

Lists and settings prove the connection; only a real message proves the chain. This is a throwaway smoke test, not the real testing — that comes after you’ve rebuilt your automations.

A few threads that ManyChat already owned can stay assigned to it even after a clean removal. Ask that person to send you a new message and Meta reassigns the thread to LinktoDM automatically. New conversations are unaffected.

All three lists showing LinktoDM and nothing else, its Page permissions on, LinktoDM set as the default routing app, and one test comment that came back with both a public reply and a DM. The switch is done; the rest is your automations.

title: Rebuild Your ManyChat Automations in LinktoDM
html:
Rebuild Your ManyChat Automations in LinktoDM

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Almost everything you ran on Instagram in ManyChat has a direct equivalent here, usually with fewer clicks, because LinktoDM only has Instagram and Facebook to think about. Rebuild the logic rather than trying to carry the old automation across — the ManyChat structure (trigger, public reply, opening DM, button, follow-up) maps onto LinktoDM’s editor step for step.

What replaces what

Section titled “What replaces what”
In ManyChat In LinktoDM
Auto-DM from comments Post automation
Keyword trigger on a comment Specific Word trigger — plus Any Word, and Intent Match for “any comment that means this”
Public reply under the comment Public comment reply, written by you or generated by AI
Several reply variations Message variations, picked at random
Opening DM Opener message
DM with buttons and links Text, buttons and attachments — up to 10 buttons, images, video, GIFs and carousels
Follow-up message after a button Follow-ups with conditions
Delay between steps Delay, or the Delay node in a flow
Story reply automation Story automation — replies, reactions and mentions
Keyword automation in DMs Chat automation
Flow Builder Flow builder, or describe the flow and let AI build it
Collecting email or phone in a flow Collect email and phone number
Tags and custom fields Tags and custom fields, with Zapier triggers when they change

Start with Create an Instagram Comment-to-DM automation for the common case; it walks the editor end to end.

Worth adding while you’re here

Section titled “Worth adding while you’re here”

A few things have no ManyChat counterpart, so porting your old flow one-for-one leaves them on the table:

  • Ask to Follow — hold the DM until the commenter follows you.
  • Backtrack comments — run a new automation back over comments already sitting on the post, up to 7 days old.
  • One automation across every post — set it to apply to all posts and reels, or to your next post, instead of wiring one automation per post.
  • Intent Match — describe what a comment should mean instead of guessing every spelling of it.

What doesn’t move across

Section titled “What doesn’t move across”

LinktoDM is built for Instagram, with Facebook Pages and Messenger alongside it. If your ManyChat account also ran WhatsApp, SMS, Telegram or email broadcasts, those have no equivalent here and are the one part of a migration that needs a different plan. There’s a fuller side-by-side on the LinktoDM vs ManyChat comparison page.

You should now have

Every automation from your notes rebuilt in LinktoDM, with the ManyChat features that have no equivalent here identified rather than discovered later.

title: After Migrating from ManyChat: Test, Backtrack and Close the Old Account
html:
After Migrating from ManyChat: Test, Backtrack and Close the Old Account

3 min read·Updated Sep 9, 2026

The automations are rebuilt, but a migration isn’t finished until you’ve seen one run. Four things, in this order.

Test from a second Instagram account

Section titled “Test from a second Instagram account”

Not the one you connected — Instagram won’t DM you your own comment, so testing from the connected account looks like a broken automation when nothing is wrong.

Comment the keyword on the post from a second account and follow the whole path through: public reply, then the DM, then the button, then whatever comes after it. Check each step against the notes you took from ManyChat. Do this for every automation you rebuilt, not just the first one.

Pick up the comments you missed

Section titled “Pick up the comments you missed”

Your old automation stopped the moment ManyChat lost the account, so anything commented between then and now went unanswered. Backtrack comments runs your new automation over comments already on the post, up to 7 days back — which usually covers the whole changeover.

Run it once the automation has tested clean, not before. Backtracking a misconfigured automation sends the wrong DM to everyone who commented that week.

Read the first busy day correctly

Section titled “Read the first busy day correctly”

New DMs go out through the sending queue rather than all at once, so a burst of comments drains over a few minutes rather than landing instantly. That’s throttling working as intended — it’s what keeps a new connection from being action-blocked — not a fault to report. You can watch what’s waiting in In queue in the console sidebar.

If something doesn’t fire

Section titled “If something doesn’t fire”

The symptom tells you where to look:

  • Public reply lands, no DM. The connection is fine and the DM step isn’t. Start from Instagram automation is not working.
  • Nothing happens at all, or you see a “not the thread owner” error. A connection survived the disconnect somewhere. Re-run the five checks on Verify the switch first, then Another app is controlling your conversations, which covers the Facebook and Instagram sides both.
  • An error mentioning the messaging API. See Fix the Instagram messaging API error.

Close ManyChat when you’re sure

Section titled “Close ManyChat when you’re sure”

Nothing of yours is left in ManyChat. The Instagram account came out on step one and its automations went with it, so what remains is a subscription still billing you for an empty account.

Wait until your rebuilt automations have run for a few days before you close it, though. While the ManyChat account still exists you can reconnect Instagram to it, which is your way back if the switch goes badly. Once it’s deleted, that door is shut.

Then, in ManyChat, Settings → Delete Account. Leave Account on the same page hands it to a teammate instead, if the account isn’t only yours.

Keep your notes and screenshots even after it’s gone. They’re the only record of what those automations said, and they cost nothing to keep.

You should now have

Every rebuilt automation tested end to end from a second account, the comments from the changeover picked up by backtrack, and the ManyChat account closed rather than quietly billing you.

title: How to Fix Instagram Automation Not Working
html:
How to Fix Instagram Automation Not Working

Updated Sep 9, 2026

If your Instagram automations are set up but nothing is firing, it’s almost always a missing Instagram permission. Before removing anything, it’s worth looking at what Instagram actually granted — a single switch is often the whole problem, and turning it back on is quicker than a full reconnection.

Do this in a desktop browser, on the same screen as your LinktoDM console.

Step 1: Open Apps and websites

Section titled “Step 1: Open Apps and websites”

Log in to instagram.com as the account you connected, then open Apps and Websites.

Stay on the Active tab and find our app. It appears as LinktoDM or as Salesmorph — both are ours.

Step 2: Check what’s actually granted

Section titled “Step 2: Check what’s actually granted”

Click View and edit. This is the screen worth reading before you change anything: it lists each permission separately, and an automation that fires for nothing usually has one of them switched off.

Which switch matters depends on what’s broken:

Switched off What stops working
Access your business message information Every DM — comment-to-DM, chat automations, follow-ups
Access your business comment information Comment triggers, so nothing fires at all
Publish content as a business Public comment replies
Access your basic business information Cannot be switched off; it’s marked Required

Switch on anything that’s off, click Save, and re-run a test automation. If that fixes it, you’re done — there’s no need to reconnect.

Step 3: Remove the connection

Section titled “Step 3: Remove the connection”

Only if everything was already on and automations still don’t fire. Back on the Active tab, click Remove and confirm. The entry moves to the Removed tab.

On the phone instead

The same screens are under Settings and activity → App website permissions → Apps and websites, then View and edit.

Step 4: Reconnect with full access

Section titled “Step 4: Reconnect with full access”

Do this straight after the removal, in the same browser session.

  1. Log out of your LinktoDM account.
  2. Log back in and reconnect Instagram (do not use email login; use Facebook/Instagram OAuth).
  3. When Meta prompts for permissions, make sure all permissions are checked before continuing. One unchecked box puts you straight back at Step 2, with a connection that looks healthy and an automation that doesn’t fire.

After reconnecting

Section titled “After reconnecting”

Comment your trigger word on a post with an active automation, from a second account, and confirm both the public reply and the DM arrive. If they still don’t, check whether another app is controlling your conversations or contact LinktoDM support with a screenshot of your View and edit screen.

title: Comment Automation Not Working: The Comment Is Invalid for a Private Reply
html:
Comment Automation Not Working: The Comment Is Invalid for a Private Reply

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Your automation is published, someone commented, and nothing was delivered. Instagram returned “the comment is invalid for a private reply”.

The message is Instagram’s, not LinktoDM’s. It means Instagram examined that specific comment and refused to let any app DM the person who wrote it.

Why a comment gets refused

Section titled “Why a comment gets refused”

There are four reasons, and they’re worth knowing apart because only two of them are fixable.

Reason Fixable?
The comment is more than 7 days old Only by acting sooner
A private reply was already sent to that comment No — and that’s correct behaviour
The comment was deleted between the trigger and the send No
The commenter’s privacy settings block message requests No, by anyone

Seven days is Instagram’s own limit on private replies, which is why backtrack also stops at seven days. A comment on a post that resurfaced weeks later can’t be answered by DM, however healthy your connection is.

A private reply is one-per-comment. If the person comments five times, only the first comment can carry the DM. This is also why One DM per user exists — without it, four of those five attempts are guaranteed failures.

Some people simply cannot be DM’d. Instagram lets users refuse message requests from accounts they don’t follow. When that’s on, no tool can reach them — LinktoDM, ManyChat or anything else. Some proportion of every audience is in this category, so a small number of these errors is normal rather than a fault.

See Public reply sent but no DM for how to tell “normal” from “broken”.

If it’s failing on every comment

Section titled “If it’s failing on every comment”

One-off failures are the reasons above. Every comment failing is a different problem, and there are three to work through in order.

1. Refresh your Instagram permissions

Section titled “1. Refresh your Instagram permissions”

Expired or partial permissions are the single most common cause of a comment-to-DM automation that fires and then delivers nothing. Remove the app access and reconnect with every permission checked — Instagram automation not working has the steps.

2. Remove every other connected app

Section titled “2. Remove every other connected app”

Instagram hands messaging control to one app at a time. If ManyChat, AnyChat or any other DM tool is still connected, it holds thread ownership and your private replies fail even though the comment itself is perfectly valid.

Remove them from both places — Meta Business Suite and Instagram’s Apps and websites list. Removing from one side is not enough: Another app is controlling your conversations walks both.

This is worth doing even if you think you already did it. Apps connected during a trial months ago stay connected until you remove them.

3. Check the account is still eligible

Section titled “3. Check the account is still eligible”

An account switched back from Professional to Personal, or unlinked from its Facebook Page, loses messaging access entirely. See the Messaging API error for the eligibility checklist.

Section titled “Escalating to Meta”

If permissions are fresh, no other app is connected, the account is eligible, and every comment still fails, the problem is on Meta’s side and LinktoDM can’t resolve it from here.

  • The error code and subcode Instagram returned, copied exactly
  • A timestamp for a specific failed attempt, with your timezone

  • What you’ve already ruled out — permissions refreshed, other apps removed, account eligible

A public reply going out with no DM behind it looks identical whether the DM was refused or the DM step is switched off. Open the automation and confirm the DM is enabled first — it’s a two-second check that saves a support thread.

title: Public Reply Sent but No DM Arrives
html:
Public Reply Sent but No DM Arrives

Updated Sep 9, 2026

The public reply appearing is proof that the automation triggered, matched the keyword and reached Instagram. So the trigger, the keyword and the connection are all fine — the failure is in the DM step alone, and there are only a few places it can be.

Work down these in order; the first two account for most cases.

1. The DM is switched off

Section titled “1. The DM is switched off”

Disable direct message turns an automation into a public-reply-only automation. It’s a setting people switch on to test the comment side and then forget.

Open the automation and confirm the DM step is enabled. This takes seconds and rules out the most embarrassing cause.

2. It arrived, in Message Requests

Section titled “2. It arrived, in Message Requests”

This is the big one, and it isn’t a fault.

Instagram files a message from an account you don’t follow into Message requests rather than the main inbox. The DM was delivered; the recipient hasn’t seen it — message requests are a tab most people check rarely, if at all. No setting on any platform changes where that first message lands.

What actually helps:

  • Send an opener message first. A short greeting with a button gets the recipient to interact, and once they do, the conversation moves into the main inbox — with your real content arriving there instead. This is the single most effective fix on this page.
  • Say in the caption that the DM is coming. “Check your message requests” in the public reply costs nothing.

Before assuming a failure, test from a second account that doesn’t follow you and check its Message requests tab. Most “no DM” reports end here.

3. The recipient can’t be reached

Section titled “3. The recipient can’t be reached”

Some people cannot receive your DM at all:

  • They’ve blocked message requests from accounts they don’t follow.
  • Their account is deactivated, restricted or deleted — Instagram returns “no matching user found” or “this person isn’t available right now”.
  • They archived or deleted the conversation mid-flow, so a follow-up has nowhere to land.

None of these are fixable, by LinktoDM or anyone else. A small proportion of every audience falls into this group, so a handful of these on a busy post is normal. See Comment automation not working for the underlying error.

4. It’s still in the queue

Section titled “4. It’s still in the queue”

A post that takes off generates more private replies than Instagram’s 750 per hour limit allows, so LinktoDM holds the surplus and releases it into the next hour rather than throwing it away. The public replies aren’t capped the same way, which is exactly why you see comment replies with no DMs behind them yet.

Open the In queue panel to check — Check your DM queue status explains what a rising count means, and rate limits and throttling covers why.

5. The 24-hour window closed

Section titled “5. The 24-hour window closed”

If the DM step is behind a delay or a follow-up longer than 24 hours, Instagram will refuse it — messaging is only allowed for 24 hours after the person’s last interaction. Shorten the delay.

Telling normal from broken

Section titled “Telling normal from broken”
What you see Verdict
Some commenters get DMs, some don’t Normal. Message requests and unreachable recipients
DMs arrive minutes or hours late during a spike Normal. The queue is working
Nobody gets a DM, on any automation Broken. Start with comment automation not working
It worked yesterday, nothing today Broken. Usually permissions or a password change

title: DMs Arrive but the Auto-Reply Doesn't Send
html:
DMs Arrive but the Auto-Reply Doesn't Send

Updated Sep 9, 2026

Messages are landing in your Instagram inbox and the chat automation isn’t answering them. Unlike a comment automation, there’s no public reply to tell you whether the trigger fired at all — so work down these in order.

1. The keyword didn’t match

Section titled “1. The keyword didn’t match”

By far the most common cause, and the least obvious, because the message looks like it should have matched.

  • Check the exact keyword. Open the automation and read the trigger field. book and Book are the same to LinktoDM, but book and boook are not.
  • Check “Trigger keyword within a sentence as well”. With this unchecked, the message must be the keyword and nothing else — so “hey can I book?” won’t match book. It’s on by default; if someone turned it off, this is your answer. See how loosely they match.
  • Watch for emoji and punctuation. People send book!! and book 🙌, which the in-sentence setting handles and strict matching does not.
  • Add the variants. Commas separate them: book, booking, appointment.

If you want the automation to answer everything regardless, switch Any word on in the same settings popover — that’s what it’s for.

2. The automation isn’t published

Section titled “2. The automation isn’t published”

A chat automation that was edited and left open is still a draft. Reopen it and confirm it’s published, and that its toggle is on in the Automations list.

If you have several chat automations, check whether an earlier one with Any word enabled is catching every message before the specific one gets a look. Two automations answering the same inbox is the usual cause of “the wrong reply goes out”.

3. Another app owns the thread

Section titled “3. Another app owns the thread”

Instagram gives messaging control to one app at a time. If ManyChat or a similar tool is still connected, it holds your conversations and LinktoDM sits in standby — comment automations may keep working while inbox replies silently don’t.

Remove the other app from both Meta Business Suite and Instagram: Another app is controlling your conversations.

4. Message access is switched off

Section titled “4. Message access is switched off”

If Instagram’s Allow access to messages switch is off, no tool can read your inbox — so nothing fires and nothing errors visibly. Fix DM access disabled.

5. The conversation is older than 24 hours

Section titled “5. The conversation is older than 24 hours”

Instagram allows replies for 24 hours after the person’s last message. A script that stalled waiting for an answer, or a message you’re only now getting to, may be outside the window — the automation isn’t broken, the door is.

6. Permissions expired

Section titled “6. Permissions expired”

If nothing above applies, refresh permissions and reconnect: Instagram automation not working.

Test with the exact string

Send yourself the keyword from a second account, character for character, with no other words. If that fires and a real sentence doesn’t, the problem is matching settings — not the connection.
